title: Tiong Bahru Estate: Singapore's first public housing
transcript:
Stand at the corner where Tiong Bahru Road meets Tiong Poh Road and look up. The pale block in front of you, with its rounded corners and long horizontal bands, was the first block of flats built on this estate. It was finished at the end of 1936, and it marks the start of a story that most people in Singapore now live inside: the story of public housing. This is Tiong Bahru Estate.

The name is a small history lesson of its own. It joins two languages. Tiong is usually explained as the Hokkien word for a tomb or cemetery, and Bahru is the Malay word for new. Put together, Tiong Bahru means something like the new cemetery. Long before anyone thought of flats here, this was a landscape of low hills, swampy hollows and graves on the edge of the town. Squatters lived among the graves in crowded wooden huts. Some kept pigs, and many worked as labourers.

In the early twentieth century, the centre of Singapore was in trouble. Chinatown was badly overcrowded, roads and drains were poor, and disease spread easily. The colonial government's answer was a new body called the Singapore Improvement Trust, created by law in 1927. Its task was to improve the town, and over time that came to mean building homes.

Tiong Bahru became the Trust's test case. The land was acquired in the late 1920s and then prepared over several years. Around two thousand squatters were moved off the site and their huts pulled down. Graves were dug up and moved elsewhere, the hills were cut down, and the earth was used to fill the swampy ground. Roads, drains and culverts followed. It was slow and costly work, and when it was done the Trust tried to sell the land to private builders. Almost nobody wanted it. The economy was only just recovering from a slump, and so in the middle of the 1930s the Trust decided to build the housing itself.

The architect most often credited with the look of the pre war blocks is the Trust's Alfred G. Church. What he and his colleagues produced was unlike anything else on the island at the time. The style is usually called Streamline Moderne, a late branch of Art Deco that loved speed and machines. Look for the curved corners, the flat roofs, and the long horizontal lines that seem to pull the building sideways, as if it were moving. Residents found their own comparison. The rounded forms reminded them of the control tower at Kallang Airport, and the flats picked up a nickname that means aeroplane houses.

The first blocks also kept something familiar. Their plan was a reworked version of the shophouse, with shops on the ground floor and homes above, along with back lanes, air wells and small courtyards that let light and air into the flats. Staircases wind down the backs of the blocks. Some window and door frames were fitted with green tinted glass, meant to soften the hard tropical light.

The first families moved in as that first block was completed at the end of 1936. There were eleven households. The rent was around twenty dollars a month or a little more, depending on the floor. That was steep for the clerks and labourers the scheme was meant to help, so the early estate tended to attract people with steadier incomes. Even so, it grew quickly. By 1941 there were 784 flats, along with fifty four tenements and thirty three shops, and more than six thousand people called Tiong Bahru home.

Then came the war. Even before the fighting reached Singapore, the planners had built shelters into the estate. One of them, at Block 78 on Guan Chuan Street, is described as the first air raid shelter built inside a public housing estate in Singapore. When the Japanese attack came, some roofs here were damaged by bombing. During the occupation that followed, the estate filled up. People moved in to escape harder conditions elsewhere, tenants sublet their rooms, and the number of residents is thought to have roughly doubled.

After the war, the Trust went back to building, and the second phase of Tiong Bahru looks quite different. By 1954 it had added 1,258 more flats, mostly on the northern side of the estate. These blocks follow the International Style. They are longer and plainer slabs, set among lawns and footpaths, with their severe lines softened by rounded balconies, round porthole windows and spiral staircases on the outside. The planners drew on the new towns being built in Britain, places such as Stevenage, Harlow and Crawley, with their idea of homes set among green space and everyday services. By the late 1950s, around seventeen thousand people lived on the estate.

Tiong Bahru was always more than flats. Its planners gathered a market, coffee shops, hawkers and a Chinese temple around a central area, and the estate is linked to several early firsts, including one of the first community centres in Singapore and the first polyclinic. It also had a reputation. Some of the flats were home to cabaret workers and to the mistresses of wealthy men, and the estate picked up a teasing nickname that translates roughly as the den of beauties.

The street names are worth reading as you walk. They honour Chinese merchants and philanthropists of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Roads here carry the names of Khoo Tiong Poh, Koh Eng Hoon and Seah Eu Chin. Kim Pong Road is said to remember Low Kim Pong, whose firm was once the largest seller of medicines on the island. Together, the signs read like a list of the people who helped build the colonial town that this estate was meant to relieve.

The Singapore Improvement Trust was later replaced by the Housing and Development Board. Tiong Bahru passed into its care, and over time many of the pre war flats were sold to the families living in them. Beside the newer towns, with their taller blocks, the old estate began to look modest and old fashioned, and for years people debated what should happen to it.

The answer came in 2003, when the Urban Redevelopment Authority gave conservation status to twenty blocks of the pre war flats. The decision recognised more than the buildings. It recognised the way of living they were designed for: green open spaces, covered walkways along the shop fronts, and shops and services on the ground floor, right below people's homes.

In the years since, Tiong Bahru has changed again. Cafes, bookshops and small boutiques have moved into the ground floor units, and flats that were once hard to let have sold for around a million dollars. Some visitors come for the coffee and hardly notice the architecture. But the architecture is the reason this place exists at all.

As you walk on, look for the small details: the curve of a stairwell, a round window, the name on a street sign. Each one belongs to the moment when a colonial trust, an old burial ground and an overcrowded town came together to try something new. What began here as an experiment became the starting point for the public housing that now shapes daily life across Singapore.

title: Tiong Bahru Market: from wooden shed to community dining room
transcript:
Look at the building on the corner of Lim Liak Street and Seng Poh Road. It is made of concrete and has two storeys. Fresh produce is sold on the ground floor, and cooked food is served upstairs. The people who planned it gave parts of it an Art Deco look, to echo the flats around it. This is Tiong Bahru Market, and the building you see opened in 2006. The story of what stood here before is much older.

First, the names. Today it is Tiong Bahru Market. For a long time it was Seng Poh Road Market, and some sources call it Seng Poh Market. Seng Poh Road is said to be named after Tan Seng Poh, Singapore's first Chinese Municipal Commissioner.

The market exists because the neighbourhood grew. Tiong Bahru was a new housing estate built by the colonial Singapore Improvement Trust. Many of the families who moved in had come from crowded Chinatown, and they needed somewhere to buy food.

At first they had a temporary market. It was a row of sheds built in 1940. By the late 1940s it was an eyesore and a fire hazard, and it was far too small. One account also says that in 1945 two shophouses on Tiong Poh Road were turned into a wet market. Meanwhile the estate kept expanding. In 1948 the government began more than a dozen extra blocks, ready from the middle of 1949. In September 1949 came plans for eighteen more blocks across Tiong Bahru and the neighbouring Alexander estate. By December 1949 the municipality had decided that the estate needed a permanent, larger market along Seng Poh Road.

Building began in 1950. Most accounts say it was finished by the end of that year and open by 1951, though one account gives 1955, so dates differ. Either way, it was plain. It was a wooden structure with a zinc pitched roof. Meat was hung without refrigeration, and bargaining over prices was normal. It served not only Tiong Bahru but also Bukit Merah and Henderson, and its stalls sold everything from textiles to flowers. Crucially, it was built with space for cooked food stalls. It was meant to bring in the street hawkers who had been serving the growing community from the roadside.

To see why that mattered, you need the wider story of hawkers. Under colonial rule, officials saw street food sellers as a problem of crowding, dirt and disease. They began licensing hawkers. The rules covered wandering hawkers from 1915 and daytime stall hawkers from 1919. From 1928 the number of licences was capped at six thousand. It did not work. Shophouse owners, especially coffee shop owners, complained that unlicensed hawkers set up near their doors without paying rent or licence fees. By 1950, after the war and with high unemployment, there were around twenty thousand unlicensed hawkers. A Hawker Inquiry Commission was set up in April 1950, in the same year the building work started here. It proposed a licensing scheme with inspectors, but the scheme came three years later, and a proper Markets and Hawkers Department only arrived in 1957. The market was part of a larger search for an orderly home for the trade.

The market also did more than sell food. In its early days it served as a kind of town hall. In March 1951, residents gathered here to decide whether Tiong Bahru should have a community centre. It was a polling centre for the Legislative Council elections of 1951 and the City Council elections of 1953. In the 1960s, political rallies were held here too.

Singapore's policy on hawkers changed over the next two decades. In 1966 the Hawkers Code barred hawking on busy roads, in daytime car parks and near schools. A registration exercise finished in 1969 with about twenty four thousand registered hawkers. A committee to plan hawker centres was set up in 1971, and in 1972 the new Ministry of Environment took over the work. It announced ten new hawker centres by 1975. From 1971 to 1986, the government aimed to move up to eighteen thousand hawkers into markets and hawker centres with proper facilities. By the end of 1986 there were 113 hawker centres across the island. One heritage account lists Tiong Bahru Market among the early hawker centres built to serve housing estates.

By the 1970s the old market badly needed repair. It looked old and dirty, and street hawkers again lined its pavements. Yet its food was gaining a name. By then it was known for Chinese breakfast foods and local specialities, and there was only one Malay stall. In the 1980s it fed nurses from the general hospital in the morning, and office workers at lunch.

The old building was a single storey with a triangular plan. Its cooked food stalls ringed a courtyard, in a hawker centre behind the market that was officially called Lim Liak Street Hawker Centre, at Block 84A. When the whole place was revamped in 1993, it took the name Tiong Bahru Market. Around 2001 the National Environment Agency began a national programme to upgrade ageing hawker centres, and this market was among those upgraded.

The biggest change came between 2004 and 2006. The market and food centre closed, and the old building was replaced. Stallholders moved to a temporary site on Kim Pong Road during the work. The new building, completed in May 2006, has lifts, escalators and bigger stalls. That is the one you are looking at.

In December 2020, UNESCO added Hawker Culture in Singapore to its list of intangible cultural heritage. It was the country's first entry on the list. Hawker centres have been called the nation's community dining rooms. Long before that phrase existed, this corner was already a place where a neighbourhood shopped, ate, voted and argued about what it needed next.

title: Tiong Bahru Air Raid Shelter: a play space built for war
transcript:
Look along Guan Chuan Street at the long, curved block of flats. This is Block 78, and it is shaped a little like a horse-shoe. It straddles two streets, Moh Guan Terrace and Guan Chuan Street. The part you are facing has something the other blocks in the estate lack. Underneath it, below the shops and the homes, is a shelter built to protect ordinary families from bombs.

Tiong Bahru was Singapore's first big public housing experiment, run by the Singapore Improvement Trust, a colonial body that was the forerunner of today's Housing and Development Board. Work on the estate began in March 1936. By 1941 it held hundreds of flats and shops, and more than six thousand people lived here. The shelter is part of the story of how that community met the war.

To see why it exists, go back to 1939. Singapore had a few air raid shelters already, built in the mid 1930s at Bukit Tunggal in Novena. Then war broke out in Europe, and people began pressing the government for more shelters. The government hesitated. Most of the city sat on low, flat ground close to the water table, so digging deep shelters would be difficult and expensive. Instead, it encouraged people to build their own and offered plans.

The Improvement Trust took a quieter route. On 28 June 1939, it announced that the new block at Guan Chuan Street would have a basement floor. In normal times it would be a covered play area for children. In an emergency, it could readily become an effective air raid shelter. Think about that for a moment. The same space was meant for children's games and for hiding from aircraft.

Records differ on the dates. One account puts the construction of the block between 1939 and 1940, another between 1939 and 1941. Records also differ on size. One account says the shelter could hold up to 1,600 people, while a newspaper report from 1941 spoke of room for two thousand. What the accounts agree on is that it was large, and that it was solid. One report from 1940 describes concrete floors and walls nineteen inches thick. That is almost half a metre of masonry.

Another account says the space was made from three play pavilions and four garages. Together they covered around fifteen hundred square metres. Heritage researchers also think it may have served as a depot for the air raid wardens, the volunteers who looked after civil defence in a neighbourhood.

Now look at the ground floor of the block, near numbers 41 and 43 Guan Chuan Street. A former resident, Nicholas Tang, who grew up in Tiong Bahru, recalled that the original entrances were here, in front of a coffee shop. When the siren sounded, two doors opened. A ladder at each doorway led down into the shelter.

The siren did sound. On 8 December 1941, Japanese aircraft attacked Singapore. Another former child resident, Linda Koh, remembered the shelter being used that day. She recalled that the inside was roomy but dark, with no ventilation. By her memory there were fewer than a hundred people inside, because the estate was not yet crowded. They waited about twenty minutes until the siren stopped.

The shelter also saw one of the stranger stories of the war. Mary Pereira says she was born in this shelter during an air raid in 1942. The shelter had medical facilities, and a doctor was on site to attend to her. Decades later, she shared that story at the launch of a heritage trail for the estate.

Even so, one account says the shelter was seldom used, because Tiong Bahru was not a major target for Japanese bombs. That did not mean the estate escaped. Roofs of several flats were damaged by the bombing, and some residents recalled at least two bombs falling on the estate. Flats were painted in camouflage colours as the war drew close. Playgrounds elsewhere in the estate were turned into makeshift shelters too.

During the Japanese Occupation, Nicholas Tang saw people use this shelter during Allied air raids in 1945. After the war, the story of the space gets less glamorous. Windows were added when it became a storage area, and for a time it was used to dump rubbish.

It was not the only one. A shelter on Eu Chin Street was later converted into a community centre, and another outhouse near Eng Watt Street was used by young boxers for training. Some homes had shelters of their own. One, in Block 74 on Tiong Poh Road, was a strong wooden structure built inside a hall, able to hold about thirty people.

Today this is described as the last remaining pre-war civilian air raid shelter in Singapore. It is also described as the first shelter built into a public housing estate, and the only Improvement Trust building designed with one. Those claims are worth treating with care, since the wording varies between accounts. But the point holds. Most of the shelters of that time are gone, and this one is still under a block of homes.

The National Heritage Board brought the shelter back into view in 2012, opening it for guided tours to mark seventy years since the Battle for Singapore. A year later, a heritage trail for Tiong Bahru launched with ten markers, and this place became one of its stops.

Before you leave, run your eye once more along the curve of the block. Ordinary families lived upstairs, and shops sat at street level. Under all of it was a space planned in 1939 for the day the sirens came. For most of the war it stayed quiet. That quiet is part of why it survives.

title: CHIJMES: the Town Convent on Victoria Street
transcript:
Look for the spire rising above the walls at the corner of Victoria Street and Bras Basah Road. It belongs to a Gothic chapel, and around it sits a whole city block of courtyards, arcades and old school buildings. For more than a century this was the Convent of the Holy Infant Jesus, a Catholic girls' school and home for nuns. Today the same grounds go by a new name, CHIJMES, pronounced like the word chimes. The name begins with CHIJ, the initials the convent went by.

Many people simply called it the Town Convent, because it sat right in the middle of the colonial town. Its story begins with a house that is still standing.

Find the building with a rounded bay that curves out towards Victoria Street. That is Caldwell House, the oldest building on the site. It went up around 1840 and 1841 as a home for H. C. Caldwell, a clerk in the colonial administration. Its architect was George Drumgoole Coleman, the first Superintendent of Public Works in Singapore, whose other works include the Armenian Church. Notice the tall French windows with louvres. They were meant to pull air through the rooms in the tropical heat.

The house became a convent because of a French priest, Father Jean-Marie Beurel of the Paris Foreign Missions Society. He wanted proper schools for the town's Catholic children. In 1851 he travelled to France to find teachers, and he won the support of the Christian Brothers and of a teaching order of nuns, the Sisters of the Holy Infant Jesus. In August 1852 he bought Caldwell House for the sisters. Accounts say he paid for it with his own money.

The first attempt went badly. Four sisters set out with Father Beurel, but their superior died after months at sea, another fell seriously ill, and a third gave up her work on reaching Singapore. So a second group came out, travelling overland across Egypt to reach Penang. From there, four sisters led by Mother Mathilde Raclot sailed south. They reached Singapore early in 1854 and moved into Caldwell House.

They wasted no time. Within about two weeks they had begun teaching. There were two classes, one for girls whose families paid fees, and one for orphans and the poor. Mother Mathilde ran the convent for around twenty years before she left for Japan, and in that time it grew into one of the largest institutions of its kind in the region.

Look again at that rounded bay. For decades its upper room served as the sisters' lounge, where they sewed, read, wrote and marked their pupils' work. A line in French can still be seen on the wall inside. It echoes the words spoken to Abraham in the Book of Genesis, walk before me, and be perfect.

The sisters are also remembered for a small door on the Victoria Street side of the convent. Babies and young children were left outside it, and the nuns took them in. Many of the babies were girls. Some were girls born in a year of the tiger, which some families believed would bring bad luck. The door came to be known as the Gate of Hope. In the mid 1850s the convent set up an orphanage, often called the Home for Abandoned Babies, where these children were raised. The gate you can see on the grounds today is a replica. The original, and the orphanage, were destroyed in the Battle of Singapore in February 1942, when Japanese bombs fell on the convent and blew out stained glass in the chapel.

Now turn to the chapel itself. The first chapel here, from the 1850s, had become so unsafe that the sisters moved their services into Caldwell House and began raising money for a new one. The design came from Father Charles Benedict Nain, a priest at the nearby Church of Saints Peter and Paul. Work started in 1901, the building was finished in 1903, and it was consecrated in June 1904. As you approach the entrance, look at the stone plaques set into the walls on either side. They carry the names of the donors who paid for it.

When the First World War broke out, he enlisted for military service and was posted to a medical unit. He died in France, and a plaque inside the chapel remembers him. His name is also among those on the bronze plates of the Cenotaph.

The chapel is built in a Gothic Revival style. A spire five storeys high marks the entrance, with flying buttresses on either side. Inside, the stained glass was made in Bruges, in Belgium, by the craftsman Jules Dobbelaere. The windows at the far end show scenes from the life of Jesus, from the Annunciation to his finding in the Temple, while panels along the sides depict the Twelve Apostles.

Before you go in, look closely at the tops of the columns, both in the chapel and along the covered walkways outside. Each capital is carved with its own mix of tropical plants and birds. By one count there are 648 of them, and no two are said to be the same.

The convent kept growing. In 1933 it took over four old bungalows that had once been the Hotel van Wijk and opened Saint Nicholas Girls' School in them. During the Japanese occupation, about forty sisters, orphans and teachers were sent to a camp at Bahau in Malaya, where many died. After the war, the schools carried on.

In the early 1980s the government acquired the land, and the schools moved to Toa Payoh. The last mass in the chapel was said on 3 November 1983, and the building was then deconsecrated.

On 26 October 1990, the chapel and Caldwell House were gazetted as national monuments. Restoration began in 1991 and took more than five years, at a cost reported as around a hundred million dollars. A specialist from France's historic monuments service helped oversee the repair of the stained glass. In 1996 the grounds reopened as CHIJMES, with the chapel renamed CHIJMES Hall. In 2002 the project received a merit award in the UNESCO Asia Pacific Heritage Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation.

Today the courtyards are given over to dining, and the chapel serves as a hall rather than a place of worship. But the plan of the old convent is still here. Walk the arcades, find the plaques by the chapel door, look for the replica gate, and remember the nuns who crossed a desert to teach in this place.

title: Victoria Theatre and Concert Hall: two halls and a clock tower
transcript:
Find the tall clock tower. Below it, two long classical buildings stretch out to either side, joined so neatly that they look like one. They are not. They were built more than forty years apart, for different reasons, and under different names. One half is the Victoria Concert Hall, once the Victoria Memorial Hall, with a statue standing before it. The other half is the Victoria Theatre, which began life as the Town Hall. Together they make up one of the oldest performing arts venues in Singapore.

Start with the older half. In the 1850s, the colony needed a proper public building. Plays and gatherings had been held in the Assembly Rooms, a simple structure with an attap roof that had fallen into poor repair. The foundation stone for a new Town Hall was laid in 1855, and the building was finished in 1862. It was paid for partly by the British administration and partly by public donations. The engineer behind it was John Bennett, and he chose a Victorian revival look with Italianate windows, then fashionable in Britain.

The Town Hall did many jobs at once. It held a theatre, offices for the municipal government and space for social events. Accounts differ on which floor held what. For its first fourteen years it also housed the Singapore Library. As the town grew, so did the demand for entertainment, and the building could not serve as both an office block and a stage. By 1893 the offices had moved out.

Now turn to the other half. Queen Victoria died in January 1901. Across the empire, people looked for ways to remember her, and in Singapore the answer was a new public hall. The Governor called for contributions, and both the government and the public gave generously. The foundation stone was laid in August 1902, as part of the celebrations for the coronation of King Edward VII. Building work ran from 1903 to 1905.

A first plan came from Major Alexander Murray and the Public Works Department. The design was then reworked by Regent Alfred John Bidwell of the architects Swan and Maclaren, and some sources credit the hall to him alone. On 18 October 1905, Governor Sir John Anderson declared the Victoria Memorial Hall open. Inside, electric fans cooled the room, so a large crowd could gather in some comfort.

Look up at the tower again. It rises about fifty four metres and ties the two halls together with a shared corridor. The Straits Trading Company donated the clock and its bells, but the gift took time to arrive, and the timepiece was only fitted after the tower itself. The clock is around four metres across, weighs about a tonne, and cost six thousand dollars. On 1 February 1907, the Duchess of Connaught set it going. The tower was also placed in line with Anderson Bridge, which carries the road over the river close by.

The fundraising for the Memorial Hall had brought in more than it cost, and the surplus went to the old Town Hall. From 1906 it was remodelled into a proper theatre, and its front was rebuilt to mirror the new hall. That is why the two wings match today. The building reopened on 11 February 1909 as the Victoria Theatre, with The Pirates of Penzance as its first show.

The style is Neoclassical. Notice the tall Corinthian columns and the triangular pediments above them, which now carry the State Crest of Singapore. Look too for oval shields marked with the letters V, R and I. They stand for Victoria, Regina and Imperatrix, Latin for Victoria, Queen and Empress.

Now the statue in front of the concert hall. This is Stamford Raffles, the British official remembered as the founder of modern Singapore. The bronze was made by the sculptor Thomas Woolner and first unveiled in 1887 on the open field then called the Esplanade, now the Padang, to mark Queen Victoria's Jubilee, fifty years after her coronation. Stray footballs struck it, and spectators climbed on it to get a better view. So in 1919, for the centenary of the founding of modern Singapore, it was moved here to Empress Place, set off by a curved colonnade and a pool.

War changed all of this. During the Battle of Singapore, the Memorial Hall became a hospital for people hurt in Japanese bombing raids. During the occupation, the Victoria Theatre became a centre of cultural life for the Japanese community, while performances went on in the Memorial Hall. The Raffles statue was taken down and stored in the museum, amid fears it would be melted for its metal. The colonnade did not survive. In 1946 the statue came back to this spot, without it.

After the war, these halls saw some of the key steps toward self rule and nationhood. War crimes trials were held in the Memorial Hall from 1946 to 1947. From 1948, it was used to brief election officials and count ballot papers. From 1953, the Rendel Commission held public meetings here as it reviewed the colony's constitution. In November 1954, the People's Action Party was founded in the hall. title: National Museum of Singapore: the dome on Stamford Road
transcript:
Find a spot on Stamford Road where you can take in the whole front of the building. It is wide, white and almost perfectly balanced, and right in the middle sits a large dome covered in small overlapping tiles. This is the National Museum of Singapore. When it opened in 1887, it had a different name: the Raffles Library and Museum. It is the oldest museum in the country.

The story starts well before this building. In 1823, Stamford Raffles held a meeting about a college he hoped to found, and the idea of a library and a museum for Singapore came up there. For years, little happened. A subscription library opened at the Singapore Institution, the school now called Raffles Institution. Then, in the 1840s, the Temenggong of Johor presented two ancient gold coins to the library. That gift prompted a small museum inside the library, and an appeal for more objects.

The collection did not have a settled home. It moved to the Town Hall, the building that is now the Victoria Theatre and Concert Hall, and later to a new wing of Raffles Institution. In the 1870s the colonial government took the library and museum on and named the joint institution after Raffles. Part of the push came from London. An exhibition of colonial products had been held at South Kensington, in the building now known as the Victoria and Albert Museum, and officials in Singapore wanted a permanent display of their own.

The collections soon outgrew borrowed rooms. Around 1882 the decision was made to build, and the Colonial Engineer, Henry McCallum, drew up the plans. Work began in 1884. On 12 October 1887, the Governor of the Straits Settlements, Sir Frederick Weld, unlocked the front door. It was the Golden Jubilee year of Queen Victoria's reign. When it opened, books filled the ground floor and the museum took the floor above.

Now look at the front again. The style is called Neo-Palladian. It is a European manner that prizes symmetry, so the left side mirrors the right. Look above the windows and you will see pediments, the small triangular caps that frame them. At each end of the front block there is a much larger triangular pediment, and these carry the coat of arms of Queen Victoria. That was most likely a nod to the jubilee.

The columns and flat pilasters follow an old classical order of rank. On the ground level they are Doric, the plainest kind. On the level above they are Ionic, with scrolled tops. Inside, eight richer Corinthian columns hold up the dome.

The dome is the part most people remember. Its fish scale tiles are made of zinc. Inside, it rises about 27 metres above a round hall called the rotunda. Light falls into that hall through Victorian stained glass panels patterned with flowers and grids. There are fifty of them, and during the last major redevelopment every one was taken down, cleaned and repaired.

The early years were not easy. Animal specimens grew mould in the damp air. Termites ate into the roof until part of it became unsafe. And because the windows had no glass, dust from the street drifted in and settled over the displays.

Still, the museum kept growing. Its first purpose was natural history, and it filled with zoological specimens from Singapore and the wider region. There was talk of moving to a larger site, but this central location was thought too good to give up. Instead, a second block was built parallel to the first, behind it. It opened in February 1907, on the first day of Chinese New Year. A library wing followed in 1916, designed to match. From 1907 until 1974, the skeleton of a blue whale hung from the upper ceiling.

Around the turn of the century, the German born entomologist Karl Hanitsch led the institution. He pushed it towards scientific research, and he began collecting portraits, plans and photographs of old Singapore. That was the start of a history collection, which would one day become the museum's main subject.

During the Japanese Occupation, from 1942 to 1945, the museum took a Japanese name, Syonan Hakubutsukan. The collections came through the war largely intact, thanks to Japanese museum directors and British staff who worked to protect them.

After the war, the library and the museum began to go their separate ways. The library moved into its own red brick building next door, and around 1960, as Singapore governed itself, the museum shed the Raffles name and became the National Museum. Records differ on exactly when that name was first used, and some accounts tie it to independence in 1965. In 1972 the animal specimens left for the University of Singapore and the new Singapore Science Centre. From then on, the museum focused on history, ethnography and art.

More changes followed. After two years of restoration, the museum reopened in November 1990. In 1992 the building was gazetted as a national monument. In 1993 it was renamed the Singapore History Museum, and for the next thirteen years it carried that name.

In 2003 the museum left Stamford Road altogether, after more than a century on this site, and moved into temporary space at Riverside Point while the building was redeveloped. It returned on 7 December 2006, with President S R Nathan at the opening, and with its old name back: the National Museum of Singapore.

That redevelopment added a modern wing of glass and metal, which more than doubled the floor space. Its centrepiece is the Glass Rotunda, a fresh take on the old one. It stands 16 metres high and 24 metres across, a steel mesh drum wrapped inside a larger drum of glass. A glass passage links the new wing to the original building. It rises almost 11 metres, and it is one of the largest self supporting outdoor glass structures in the world. This passage is the only modern intrusion the Urban Redevelopment Authority allowed. Some of its beams are made of optical glass, so that people inside can still see the whole dome.

One last detail is easy to miss. The red brick National Library next door was pulled down in 2004 to make way for the Fort Canning Tunnel. Where its car park used to be, the museum built a theatre, and lined its walls with 16,720 red bricks made to look like the library's own, laid in a herringbone pattern.

Before you move on, look up at the dome again. It has watched over a reading room, a whale skeleton, a wartime renaming and a glass wing at its side. Each age of this building left a layer, and the names on the door changed with each one.

title: Raffles Hotel: from beach house to national monument
transcript:
You are standing on Beach Road, in front of one of the best known hotels in Asia. Its white walls, deep verandas and tall palms have filled postcards for well over a century, and today it is a national monument. But Raffles Hotel began as something much smaller. It started life as a rented seaside bungalow, turned into a hotel with only a handful of rooms. This is the story of how it grew.

The house that stood on this site was built in the early 1830s as a private home looking out to sea. It came to be owned by Syed Mohamed Alsagoff, a wealthy Arab merchant and landowner, who rented it out. For a few years it was run as a small hotel by a man named Charles Emerson, and after his death it was used as a boarding house for boys from Raffles Institution.

In 1887 the lease passed to four Armenian brothers, Martin, Tigran, Aviet and Arshak Sarkies. They were already in the hotel trade, with the Strand Hotel in Yangon and several hotels in Penang. They named their new venture after Stamford Raffles, the British colonial official remembered as the founder of modern Singapore. Raffles Hotel opened its doors at the start of December 1887. Accounts differ on its size, but the most common figure is just ten rooms.

The timing was good. Steamships and the opening of the Suez Canal had made the long voyage from Europe to Asia shorter and more comfortable, and a new kind of traveller was arriving: the wealthy visitor who came to see the East for pleasure. Demand soon outgrew the little hotel. New wings went up around 1889 and 1890, a billiard room followed, and in 1894 the Palm Court Wing opened in a neighbouring building. By then the hotel had around seventy five rooms.

The grand building you see in front of you came next. It was completed in 1899 on the site of the old beach house, which was pulled down to make way for it. The design was by Regent Alfred John Bidwell of the architectural firm Swan and Maclaren, and it is three storeys tall in a Neo-Renaissance style. It was modern in a way guests noticed straight away. The hotel had one of the first complete electrical systems in Singapore, running electric lights, ceiling fans and call bells from its own generators. In a hot and humid port, a fan turning overhead at the touch of a switch was a real luxury.

Through the early twentieth century, Raffles became a place to be seen. Over the decades its guest list grew to include writers, film stars and royalty. The novelist Somerset Maugham, the poet Rudyard Kipling and the comic actor Charlie Chaplin are among the names linked to the hotel. Much later came Michael Jackson, and the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. The hotel has never been shy about telling these stories, and it keeps them alive in its corridors and bars.

One of its favourite tales dates from 1902. A tiger that had escaped from a circus nearby was found sheltering in the space beneath the billiard room, and it was shot there. It is the kind of story that grows in the telling, and the hotel still enjoys telling it.

Another story belongs to the Long Bar. It was there that a bartender named Ngiam Tong Boon created the Singapore Sling, a cocktail that carried the island's name around the world. Today the drink is as much a part of the hotel's identity as its verandas.

The good times did not last. When Arshak Sarkies died in 1931, it emerged that the brothers had run up heavy debts. The Great Depression made those debts impossible to manage, and the family business went bankrupt. In 1933 a new public company, Raffles Hotel Limited, was formed and took over the hotel and its land. The name stayed. The family that had built it was gone.

Then came the Second World War. In February 1942, Singapore fell to Japanese forces. The hotel tells a story that, as the city fell, guests were dancing one last waltz, and that staff buried the hotel silver in the grounds of the Palm Court to keep it safe. Under the occupation, the hotel was given a new name, Syonan Ryokan. Syonan, meaning light of the south, was the name the Japanese gave to Singapore, and a ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn. In 1945, when the British returned, the hotel was taken back.

In the decades after the war, the hotel carried on, but it changed piece by piece. Wings were added and rooms altered. Even its famous entrance had been reshaped. The original cast iron porch at the front, put up in 1913, had been taken down in 1920 to make way for a ballroom. In 1987, in recognition of its place in the history of Singapore, Raffles Hotel was gazetted as a national monument.

Two years later, in 1989, the hotel closed for a major restoration that lasted until 1991. The aim was to bring back the look of its heyday in the years around 1915. The cast iron porch you see at the entrance today is a reproduction made during that work. An ornate cast iron fountain made by the foundry of Walter MacFarlane and Company, which had been rediscovered in 1989, was brought into the gardens. When the hotel reopened, every room had become a suite.

The hotel has changed hands several times since then. Between 2017 and 2019 it closed again for another major renovation, reopening in August 2019. Today it is run by the hotel group Accor and has more than a hundred suites.

As you stand here, picture the whole sequence. A bungalow facing the sea. A tiny hotel run by four brothers from a distant community. A palace of electric fans and long verandas. A wartime inn under another name. And finally a monument, rescued and restored. Raffles Hotel has been reinvented many times, but each version has kept the same name, and each has drawn travellers back to this spot on Beach Road.

title: The Arts House: the Old Parliament House by the river
transcript:
Before you go inside, find the bronze elephant standing on its tall pedestal in front of the building. It is easy to walk past. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to it. The white building behind it is The Arts House. For most of the twentieth century it carried a very different name. Singaporeans knew it as Parliament House, and today many still call it the Old Parliament House.

It is often described as the oldest government building in Singapore. The ground it sits on is older still. When workers refurbished the building in 1989, they found fragments of stoneware and earthenware from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, a sign that people lived along this stretch of river long before the British arrived. This riverbank is also where Stamford Raffles is thought to have come ashore at the end of January 1819. At the time, the area was home to the Temenggong Abdul Rahman and his followers. A few years later Raffles persuaded them to move to Telok Blangah, because he wanted this land for public use.

That plan is the root of the building's odd early history. In 1826, a Scottish merchant named John Argyle Maxwell, who traded out of Java, began building a grand private house here. Raffles had marked the plot for government use, but his successor, John Crawfurd, gave Maxwell a permit to build anyway. The house was finished in 1827. Its designer was George Drumgoole Coleman. Coleman later became Superintendent of Public Works and designed the Armenian Church and the first St Andrew's Church.

Coleman gave Maxwell a mansion in the Neo Palladian style. But Maxwell never lived in it. Once the authorities realised the house stood on land meant for the government, a compromise was struck. Maxwell kept the property on a very long lease, and the government rented the house from him for five hundred rupees a month. It became a courthouse. Records differ on exactly how ownership changed hands after that, but by 1842 the building belonged to the government and the East India Company.

So for much of the nineteenth century, this was a place of law. The first court sittings were held in a room on the upper floor at the front. Government offices, including the Land Office, shared the space. In 1839 a single storey courthouse went up next door, and the court moved into it. It did not stay. A boatyard nearby made so much noise that the judges went back to the main house. In 1868 the Supreme Court was set up on the premises.

title: St Andrew's Cathedral: a church built twice
transcript:
Look up at the spire rising above the grounds between Coleman Street and North Bridge Road. This is St Andrew's Cathedral, the main Anglican church of Singapore. It is the second church to stand on this ground, and the first one had a short and unlucky life. Its story, and that of the men who built its replacement, is worth hearing first.

When Stamford Raffles drew up his plan for the town in 1822, he marked out a plot here for an Anglican church. Nothing was built for over a decade. The local community had to raise the money first, and it was only in the 1830s that work could begin. Until then, Anglicans in Singapore borrowed a simple wooden chapel with an attap roof, run by the London Missionary Society near the corner of Bras Basah Road. That spot is now part of Raffles Hotel, a short walk from here.

The first church was designed by George Drumgoole Coleman, the architect and surveyor who also gave Singapore the Armenian Church. Bishop Daniel Wilson of Calcutta laid its foundation stone on 9 November 1835, and the building was finished within a year or two. Scottish residents had given generously to the building fund, so the church was named after Andrew, the patron saint of Scotland.

Coleman worked in a calm, classical style, and not everyone liked it. Some people grumbled that it looked more like a public hall or a college than a place of worship. So in 1842 a spire was added, under John Turnbull Thomson. Nobody fitted a lightning conductor. Lightning struck the spire in 1845, and again in 1849. By 1852 the church was judged unsafe and closed, and in 1855 it was pulled down. While a new church was built, the congregation went back to the old missionary chapel.

The building you see now was started under the Governor of the Straits Settlements, William Butterworth. Its designer was Lieutenant Colonel Ronald MacPherson, who held two jobs at once. He was the government's executive engineer, and he was also in charge of the convicts. That second job shaped the whole project.

From 1825, the British sent convicts from India to Singapore. Thousands of them worked on roads, drains and public buildings. They were trained as brickmakers, bricklayers and carpenters, and many of the early colonial buildings in this district were raised by their hands. MacPherson chose the Gothic Revival style. Then he simplified his own plans so that Indian convict labourers could build them more easily. Using convicts was also a way to save money. His full estimate came to around a hundred and twenty thousand rupees, but he reckoned that convict labour, and materials made by convicts, would cut the cash outlay to under fifty thousand.

Bishop Wilson came back to lay the new foundation stone on 4 March 1856. MacPherson is said to have taken ideas from Netley Abbey, a ruined medieval monastery in Hampshire, England. Inside, the piers of the nave are said to closely resemble the ones that survive there. MacPherson did not see the work through. In 1857 he was posted to Malacca, and the job passed to others, chiefly John McNair and the engineer John Bennett, with W. D. Bayliss of the public works office.

Money stayed tight. In 1859 a newspaper complained that the few convicts working as plasterers inside had been taken off the job. Even so, the church held its opening service in October 1861, and it was consecrated in January 1862. Most accounts give 1861 as the year it was finished. But one careful study found that the outside and the spire were still incomplete at that point. MacPherson's spire design was dropped and redrawn by a public works engineer named Jasper Otway Mayne. The spire was done only in December 1864, and the last work ended in April 1865.

Behind the drawings stood a convict named Babajee Rajaram, from Bombay. He led the team preparing plans for St Andrew's and other public works, and he is described as the first native draughtsman in Singapore. Convict labour here carried on until 1873, when the last Indian convicts were shipped away.

Now look at the walls. For more than a century, nearly every description of this church has mentioned Madras chunam. This was a polished lime plaster named after Madras, the Indian city now called Chennai. McNair later wrote a book about the convict system, published in 1899, and in it he described the mix. It was shell lime without sand, beaten with egg whites and a coarse sugar called jaggery, then thinned with water in which coconut husks had soaked. Once dry, the walls were rubbed with crystal or smooth stones until they shone.

It is a good story, and it may not be true. An architectural historian, Yeo Kang Shua, spent years studying plaster samples from inside the cathedral during repairs. He found no trace of egg white or coconut fibre. A newspaper report from 1949 described the old interior walls as grey, while true Madras chunam was prized for being very white. With money so short, and with plasterers pulled off the job, he argues the famous plaster was most likely never used here. He also admits that we can never be completely sure.

Now turn to the tower. The belfry, with its pointed lancet windows, has been compared to the one at Salisbury Cathedral. Below it is a covered carriage porch, built so that people arriving could step down out of the sun. The first church had a bell given in 1843 by Maria Balestier, wife of the American consul and a daughter of the American patriot Paul Revere. It was replaced by a set of bells in 1889, and the old bell is now kept at the National Museum of Singapore.

The church became a cathedral in 1870. Inside, three tall stained glass windows behind the altar honour Raffles, John Crawfurd, an early Resident of Singapore, and Governor Butterworth. Each carries the man's coat of arms. A cross on the column that holds up the pulpit is made from nails taken from the ruins of Coventry Cathedral in England, destroyed by bombing in the Second World War. A stone from Canterbury Cathedral, sent in 1936, is set into a pillar near the lectern.

War came here too. In 1942, as the Japanese advanced on Singapore, the nave was turned into an emergency hospital for the wounded. On 28 June 1973, the cathedral was gazetted as a national monument.

Before you leave, look around the grounds for a granite memorial topped with a Maltese cross. It remembers Ronald MacPherson, who designed this church and never saw it finished. An old road called Jalan Klapa was renamed MacPherson Road in his honour. Most of the convicts who built this church left no names behind. The building is their record.

title: Asian Civilisations Museum: the Empress Place Building on the river
transcript:
Face the river and then turn around. The long, pale building with the pitched tile roofs and rows of tall shuttered windows is the Empress Place Building. Today it houses the Asian Civilisations Museum, often shortened to ACM. Two names, one structure, and a story that runs from a colonial courthouse to a museum about the whole of Asia.

Start with where you are. This is the north bank of the Singapore River, right by its mouth. Its classical front caught the eye of immigrants and visitors sailing into the harbour.

The ground beneath your feet is older than any of that. Archaeologists from the National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University have dug the open land between the building and the river. They report that people were already living and working here in the early fourteenth century, and that the spot stayed in use during the time of the Melaka sultanate. A Portuguese map printed in 1604 even marks an official at Singapore whose title meant lord of the harbour, a sign that foreign merchants were still calling at this port long before the British came.

The British arrived in 1819. Close by on this same bank, a statue marks the place where tradition says Stamford Raffles stepped ashore on 28 January that year, although historians still argue about the exact spot. From then on, traffic on the river grew heavy as trade expanded, and this bank became the place where the new colony would govern itself.

The building in front of you was part of that plan. The project was approved in 1855, but work did not begin until June 1864, because the money of the Straits Settlements had been pulled away into military spending. The design came from Major John McNair, the Colonial Engineer, who was also the Superintendent of Convicts. That second job matters. The building was put up by convict labour, and the National Heritage Board says those convicts were Indian. It was finished in December 1867, and one report puts the final cost at fifty three thousand dollars, a little over the estimate.

It was first meant to be a courthouse, and it did serve the colonial court at the start. How long the court stayed is a question where records differ. One heritage account says the court soon moved out because the rooms carried sound badly. Others describe an older courthouse here that was extended toward the river and used for decades. What everyone agrees on is that the original building quickly filled up with something else: offices.

Almost the entire colonial bureaucracy ended up here. The Secretariat, the Treasury, Public Works, the Land Office and the Audit Office all had rooms in the building, along with the Colonial Engineer and the head of the police. The Legislative Council met in a large room upstairs. People simply called the place Government Offices, and for a time it was also known as the Council Chamber and Public Offices. Because the Surveyor General worked here too, the building long served as the reference point for the map coordinates of Singapore.

As the colony grew, so did the building. It was extended several times, and the last major addition came in 1920. Each new wing followed McNair's original style, which is why the whole thing still reads as one design. Then, in 1907, the open square beside it was named Empress Place, in memory of Queen Victoria, who had also held the title Empress of India. Over time the offices took the name of the square, and Government Offices became the Empress Place Building.

Now look closely at the walls. The style is Neo Palladian, a classical manner built on order and balance. The ground floor is rusticated, meaning the plaster is cut into heavy blocks to look solid. Above it run arcaded verandahs and a facade with Roman Doric columns. Notice the many French windows and timber louvres. Inside, the plan is laid out symmetrically along a central axis, and many of the original plaster mouldings and cornices survive.

In the twentieth century the building became political ground. After the Second World War it was seen as the control room of government, and it sat at the centre of the push to replace senior British officers in the civil service with qualified local people. In 1956 David Marshall, the first Chief Minister of Singapore, gave a stirring speech here calling for a Malayan Merdeka, meaning independence.

The building also touched ordinary lives. Crowds came here to register as voters for the 1959 elections, when Singapore moved to self rule, and again to register as citizens after full independence in 1965. Into the 1980s it held the Citizenship Registry, the Immigration Department and the Registry of Births and Deaths, so for many families this was simply where official papers were made.

When the government offices moved out, the building was restored and reopened on 7 April 1989 as the Empress Place Museum, opened by Ong Teng Cheong. It focused on Chinese history and art, and its first show brought royal objects from the Qing dynasty. But the museum ran into difficulties and closed in 1995. Meanwhile, in 1992, the building was gazetted as a national monument.

The Asian Civilisations Museum itself began elsewhere. It opened in 1997 in the Old Tao Nan School on Armenian Street, with a focus on Chinese civilisation, and it traces its roots further back to the Raffles Museum of the middle of the nineteenth century. In March 2003 it opened here, by the river, and widened its scope. The Armenian Street building later reopened as the Peranakan Museum.

The idea behind ACM is a pan Asian one. It deals with the material history of China, Southeast Asia, South Asia and West Asia, the regions from which the different communities of Singapore trace their ancestry, and it tells that story through the lens of Singapore as a port city. One part of its collection fits this riverbank especially well: the cargo of a ninth century trading ship found off Belitung Island in 1998, with more than sixty thousand Tang dynasty ceramics made in China.

Before you head inside or move on, look from the shuttered windows down to the water. People of the fourteenth century, colonial clerks, voters in queues, and now objects carried across Asian seas have all passed through this one stretch of riverbank.

Before you head inside or move on, look from the shuttered windows down to the water. People of the fourteenth century, colonial clerks, voters in queues, and now objects carried across Asian seas have all passed through this one stretch of riverbank.

title: National Gallery Singapore: two monuments, one museum
transcript:
Stand at the edge of the Padang with your back to the field, and look up. Two grand stone buildings stand side by side along St Andrew's Road. The one with the green dome is the former Supreme Court. It had outgrown its old rooms in the Town Hall, and in 1920 it bought land on this side of the Padang. The new Municipal Building was designed chiefly by the municipal architect Alexander Gordon. Building work ran from 1926 to 1929, and it was declared open on 23 July 1929.

Look at the front. Eighteen Corinthian columns, each three storeys tall, march across the facade above a broad flight of steps. Before land was reclaimed along this coast, the buildings facing the Padang formed a stately seafront, a show of imperial power that greeted ships sailing past. Yet the look is partly a costume. Behind the stone face is a steel frame, and the windows and rooms inside are plain and modern rather than richly decorated.

Now turn to the building with the dome. Its site once held the Hotel de l'Europe, at one time the grandest hotel in town. The hotel ran into money trouble and closed in the early 1930s, and the government took the land for a new Supreme Court. The design came from Frank Dorrington Ward, chief architect of the Public Works Department. He matched its height to City Hall, so the two would read as one civic front.

On 1 April 1937, the Governor, Sir Shenton Thomas, laid the foundation stone, said at the time to be the largest in Malaya. Beneath it lies a sealed time capsule holding six Singapore newspapers from 31 March 1937 and a handful of Straits Settlements coins. It is not due to be opened until the year 3000. Work was slowed by late deliveries of steel, as shipping was congested and Britain was rearming for war. The court finally opened on 3 August 1939, at a cost of around one point seven five million Straits dollars. It is often described as the last Neoclassical building of colonial Singapore.

Look up at the triangular pediment above the columns. That carved group is an allegory of justice by the Italian sculptor Cavaliere Rudolfo Nolli, the same man who supplied the columns for City Hall next door. In the centre sits Justice on a throne, holding a sword and scales. Two kneeling figures flank her, one asking for protection and one giving thanks. To one side are figures for deceit and violence, and lawmakers holding books. To the other is a bull, for wealth, and two children hugging sheaves of wheat, for plenty. Below, a long frieze shows scenes of early Singapore, including building work, rubber tapping, fishing, trade and the signing of the 1819 treaty that set up the British settlement.

The big copper green dome has been compared to the dome of Saint Paul's Cathedral in London. Underneath it sits a round room that was built as the court's law library. Inside, there was no marble. Corridors were laid with rubber tiles made in Singapore to look like marble, and they helped muffle footsteps near the courtrooms. The fine plaster in the main hall was done by Chinese craftsmen who had fled the war in China and had learned European plastering in Shanghai.

Within three years of the court's opening, Singapore was at war. When Japanese bombs began falling in early 1942, the Municipal Building opened its doors as a shelter. After Singapore fell in February 1942, the Japanese ran the city's affairs from inside it. Allied prisoners of war were gathered in front of it before they were marched to Changi. The court next door became the Syonan Supreme Court. In 1943, Subhas Chandra Bose, leader of the Indian National Army, rallied here for Japanese support to free India from British rule.

Then the tide turned. On 12 September 1945, in this building, Admiral Lord Louis Mountbatten accepted the surrender of Japanese forces from General Seishiro Itagaki. A victory parade filled the Padang the same day. In the years after, the Supreme Court was one of the places where Japanese soldiers faced war crime trials.

In 1951, when King George the Sixth granted Singapore city status, the Municipal Building became City Hall. Eight years later, it hosted one of the country's founding scenes. On 5 June 1959, Lee Kuan Yew and his eight ministers took their oaths in the City Hall Chamber, and he became Singapore's first Prime Minister. That December, crowds gathered outside to see Yusof bin Ishak installed as head of state, and they saw the new flag and heard the new anthem for the first time. On 16 September 1963, Lee stood on these very steps and read the Proclamation of Malaysia.

Both buildings were gazetted as national monuments in 1992. The courts moved into a new building directly behind them in 2005, and the old pair fell quiet.

The idea of turning them into a national gallery was announced that same year. A design competition followed, drawing 111 entries from 29 countries. The winner was studioMilou, working with CPG Consultants. Because the buildings were protected, key parts could not be touched, such as the facades, the room where the surrender took place, and Lee Kuan Yew's old office. Before construction, archaeologists dug on the site and found objects from the fourteenth to the nineteenth centuries, traces of trade long before the colonial town.

Work began in 2011. The two buildings were linked underground by a new basement and overhead by glass and aluminium bridges, built so they could one day be removed without harming the old stone. Above it all floats a broad roof canopy on slender, tree like supports, inspired by tropical leaves and filtering light into the space between the buildings.

The Gallery opened in November 2015. With about 64,000 square metres of floor space, it is the largest museum in Singapore, devoted to the art of Singapore and Southeast Asia from the nineteenth century to today.

A colonial city hall, a court of law, a wartime headquarters, a stage for self rule, and now a home for art. Each of those lives left its mark on this one long front facing the Padang.
