title: Thian Hock Keng: the temple that faced the sea
transcript:
Telok Ayer Street is a long way from the sea today. Between here and the water there are whole blocks of offices, roads and reclaimed land. But when this temple was built, the shoreline ran along this street, and many of the people who came to pray here had only just stepped off a boat. This is Thian Hock Keng, one of the oldest Hokkien temples in Singapore, and for generations the spiritual heart of the Hokkien community.

At its centre is Mazu, the goddess of the sea. Many of the early Chinese immigrants to Singapore came from Fujian province on the south eastern coast of China, and many of them were Hokkien. Their journey south was long and dangerous. Those who survived it came ashore at Telok Ayer Bay, and their first act on land was often to give thanks to Mazu for a safe crossing. Others came before setting out again, to ask for her protection on the voyage ahead.

Before there was a temple, there was a small shrine near the shore, set up in the early 1820s. It was modest, but it mattered. As more and more immigrants arrived, the community decided that the goddess deserved a proper home. Money was gathered over many years, and building on a permanent temple began in 1839.

It took three years. The temple was completed in 1842, at an estimated cost of thirty thousand Spanish dollars. Most of the money came from wealthy Hokkien merchants and community leaders. The largest single gift came from Tan Tock Seng, a Malacca born merchant and philanthropist. A granite tablet in the entrance hall still lists the donors, and its inscription makes a point worth noticing: the temple was meant for all Chinese, not only for one dialect group.

Much of what you see was brought from China. Building materials were shipped in, and artisans from Fujian made the carvings and decorations. According to the temple's own history, some of the stone and timber came as ballast in the holds of ships, weight that was needed for the voyage and then put to new use on land. The temple also remembers help from beyond the Chinese community. Indian workers from nearby Chulia Street are said to have helped with the building, and a small carved figure of a man holding up a beam is thought to honour them.

In 1840, while the building work was still going on, a statue of Mazu arrived from China. It was carried through the streets in a grand procession and placed in the main hall as the temple's chief deity. That same year, the Hokkien Huay Kuan, the Hokkien clan association, was set up within the temple grounds. Its aims included running schools, supporting new arrivals from Fujian, and keeping Chinese language and culture alive far from home.

Take a moment to look at the building itself. Thian Hock Keng follows a traditional Hokkien plan of three halls set one behind the other: an entrance hall, a main hall, and a rear hall, with side halls running along the edges. The roofs are the first thing most people notice. Their ridges curve upwards and end in sweeping tips shaped like a swallow's tail, and they are crowded with dragons and other figures. Many of these are made with a technique called jian nian, in which pieces of coloured porcelain are cut and set into the plaster to form a bright mosaic. At the entrance, stone lions and painted door gods stand guard.

Inside, the main hall belongs to Mazu. But she is not alone. At the back of the temple is a shrine to Guanyin, the goddess of mercy. Other altars honour Baosheng Dadi, a god of medicine, and Guan Yu, also known as Lord Guan. Confucius is honoured here too.

The temple was never only a place of worship. In 1849, a small complex called Chongwen Ge was added beside it, led by the merchant Tan Kim Seng with support from Hokkien, Hakka and Teochew donors. It is described as the first Chinese school in Singapore. In the early twentieth century, the Chong Hock Pavilion was built next to the temple, and the Hokkien Huay Kuan later started a girls' school there, one of the earliest Chinese schools for girls on the island.

The temple kept changing as the city around it changed. A renovation in 1906 added a few Western touches, including an ornamental iron gate made in Glasgow and decorative wall tiles. Then, in 1907, came the temple's highest honour. Emperor Guangxu of the Qing dynasty in China sent a plaque and a scroll to Thian Hock Keng. The four characters on the plaque, read as bo jing nan ming, can be translated as gentle waves on the southern seas. It was a fitting blessing for a temple built for sailors and immigrants, and it hangs in the main hall.

Meanwhile, the sea was moving away. From the late nineteenth century onwards, land reclamation pushed the shoreline further and further out, until the temple that once looked across the water found itself looking at streets and buildings.

In 1973, Thian Hock Keng was gazetted as a national monument. A major restoration followed much later, running from 1998 to 2000. In 2001 the work received an honourable mention in the UNESCO Asia Pacific Heritage Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation.

As you stand in front of the temple, try to picture the scene as it once was: the water close by, small boats pulled up on the shore, and tired travellers climbing the steps to light incense in thanks for their safe arrival. Thian Hock Keng was built by people who had crossed the sea to start again. It has watched the sea retreat and a city rise around it, and it still opens its doors to anyone who wants to step inside.

title: Masjid Al-Abrar: the hut mosque of the Chulias
transcript:
Look for the two slim towers rising above the row of shophouses. Each is eight sided, and each is topped with a crescent moon and a star. Between them is the entrance to Masjid Al-Abrar, one of the oldest mosques in Singapore. The building does not stand apart on its own plot. It sits shoulder to shoulder with its neighbours, as if it were simply one more shop on Telok Ayer Street.

The mosque has more than one name. Al-Abrar is an Arabic word for people who are righteous and devout. It is also called the Chulia Mosque, after the community that built it. And in Tamil it carries a humbler nickname, Kuchu Palli, which means the hut mosque. That nickname is a clue to how it began.

The mosque was founded in 1827. Its first building was a small hut with a thatched roof and walls of woven sticks plastered with mud, a method known as wattle and daub. The land beneath it was given as a waqf, a religious endowment, by an Indian Muslim merchant whose name is recorded as Hadjee Puckery Mohamed Khatib bin Shaik Mydin.

So who were the Chulias? They came from the Coromandel Coast, the south eastern shore of India. The name Coromandel is a European version of Cholamandalam, meaning the realm of the Cholas, an old dynasty of that region. For centuries the coast was a great trading region, with a chain of busy ports. Tamil Muslim trading groups from those ports, with names such as Lebbai, Rawther, Marakayyar and Kayalar, became known across Southeast Asia as the Chulia merchants.

In early colonial Singapore, the Chulias were mostly traders and moneychangers. Many of them settled and worked in what is now Chinatown, living alongside Chinese and other Indian residents. For them the mosque was more than a place of prayer. It was also where the community met, talked and kept in touch with one another.

To picture their world, you need to move the sea. Telok Ayer Street began as a coastal road running along Telok Ayer Bay, and it takes its name from that bay. In the first years of British Singapore, the street ran right along the water. Boats moored in the bay and waited for fresh water, which was brought down by bullock cart from a well at Ann Siang Hill. Temples and mosques sprang up along the shore, built by Chinese and Indian Muslim settlers who wanted to give thanks for a safe passage across the sea.

The hut did not last. In 1850, work started on a brick mosque to replace it, and the new building was finished in 1855. That is the core of the mosque you see today, although it has been enlarged since.

Within a year of its completion, the mosque appeared in a painting. In 1856 the artist Percy Carpenter painted Telok Ayer Street as seen from Mount Wallich, a hill that once stood close by. In that picture the two minarets rise clearly beside Thian Hock Keng, the Hokkien temple a little way along the street. So these towers have been a landmark here since the middle of the nineteenth century.

The Chulias built more than one place of worship in the area. The Jamae Mosque on South Bridge Road was put up in the 1830s, and it too is called the Chulia Mosque. A short walk along this street is the Nagore Dargah, a shrine the community raised to a Sufi saint whom many sailors credited with their safe voyages. Together these three sites formed the Chulia wakaf, a shared endowment. Heritage records differ on when Al-Abrar joined the other two under a single panel of court appointed trustees. One account links it to the completion of the brick building, while others place it in 1910. In 1917, all three were handed to the Mahomedan and Hindu Endowment Board.

Meanwhile, the shoreline was being pushed away. From the late 1870s, Telok Ayer Bay was filled in to make new land. Hills along the coast, Mount Wallich among them, were cut down, and their earth was used to fill in the water. Sources give different dates for when this first scheme was finished, but by its end, new streets and buildings stood between Telok Ayer Street and the sea. The waterfront mosque had become an inland one.

On 19 November 1974, Masjid Al-Abrar was gazetted as a national monument, the tenth in Singapore. After independence it had come under the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore, known by its Malay name Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura, or MUIS.

The building you are looking at owes much to a major renovation in the 1980s. Until then the mosque had only one storey. An upper floor was added, along with a large jack roof, to make the prayer hall bigger. The open courtyard between the gate and the prayer hall was covered over, creating a gallery above. Accounts of the new capacity vary, from around 800 to 900 worshippers. Later, in the 1990s, the mosque bought the shophouse next door, and that space became a prayer hall for women.

Now take a closer look at the front. The mosque is three shophouses wide. Like its neighbours, it gives up its ground floor frontage to the five foot way, the walkway that links the shophouses along this side of the street, so the path passes straight in front of the mosque without a break. Above, a parapet runs the full width of the front. It once covered only the central section. Its row of small decorative battlements, called merlon cresting, resembles the cresting on the Sultan Mosque.

There is a quiet piece of luck in the plan as well. Every mosque must face the qibla, the direction of Mecca. Here, the boundary lines of the plot happen to match that direction, so the prayer hall could follow the street grid and still face the right way.

The style draws on Indo-Islamic architecture, and that is what sets the mosque apart from the shophouses around it. But there are European touches too. Inside, the prayer hall is lined with Doric columns in the Neoclassical manner. Tall French louvred windows have coloured glass set into the fanlights above them. And over the mihrab, the niche that marks the direction of prayer, is a panel of blue glass bearing a verse of the Quran in Arabic, which opens in the name of God, the most gracious and most merciful.

One more name on the map tells this story. Not far from here, in the financial district, is Chulia Street. It was once called Kling Street, a term the Indian community found insulting, and in 1921 it was renamed after the Chulias. That street and this mosque both carry the memory of the same people, the merchants from the Coromandel Coast who once worked a few steps from the sea.

title: Nagore Durgha: a shrine for a saint of safe voyages
transcript:
Look up at the front of this building, on the corner of Telok Ayer Street and Boon Tat Street. Two square towers rise above a flat roof. Between them runs a strip of tiny arches and openings, like the front of a palace shrunk down to the size of a model. This is Nagore Durgha, also spelled Nagore Dargah. It began life as a shrine for a Muslim holy man, and it is now a national monument and the Nagore Dargah Indian Muslim Heritage Centre.

To understand why it is here, picture this street without the towers of the business district behind you. In the early years of British Singapore, Telok Ayer Street ran along the shore. Ships docked along this seafront, and many newcomers set foot on the island right here. The town plan of 1822 marked Telok Ayer out as a Chinese district, but the people who actually landed here came from many places. From the late 1800s, the British began reclaiming land from the sea. The street ended up four streets away from the water, and Cecil Street, Robinson Road and Shenton Way were laid out on the new ground.

Among those who came ashore were the Chulias. They were Tamil speakers from the Coromandel Coast of southern India, and in Singapore they worked mostly as traders and moneychangers. Many of them were Muslim. And many were devoted to a Sufi saint named Shahul Hamid, whose great shrine stands in Nagore, a town in Tamil Nadu. The saint was believed to have worked miracles, and he was especially loved by people who made their living on the water. Sailors and seafarers credited him with getting them home safely. Before leaving India for the long voyage to Singapore, Chulia travellers would visit his shrine in Nagore to ask for a safe passage.

Once settled here, they wanted a place to keep that devotion alive. So between 1828 and 1830, they built this shrine. At first it was called the Shahul Hamid Dargah. A dargah is a shrine to a holy figure, and only later did this one take the name of the saint's home town and become the Nagore Dargah. It is worth knowing that the saint is not buried here, and no relics of his body are kept inside. This building is a memorial, a way of honouring him far from Nagore. Inside there was a cenotaph shaped like a grave, and later generations came to treat it as a keramat, a sacred site.

The land itself came through a man named Kaderpillai. The records differ on the details. One account says he gave the land, while the heritage board says it was leased to him. The lease came with a condition from the British authorities. Nothing on the site could be built of attap, a palm thatch, or of wood, because of the risk of fire. According to one account, two brothers, Mohammed and Haja Mohiddeen, brought in building materials from overseas, including limestone, concrete and steel supports. The result was a solid masonry building, and today its walls are painted in peach and white.

Now take a closer look at the details. The style is a mix, drawing on several traditions at once. There are minarets and crescent and star motifs of the kind you see on mosques. But along the walls you will also find fluted pilasters with Corinthian and Doric tops, borrowed from classical European building. The overall look is often described as Indo Saracenic, a style that blends Indian, Islamic and European forms.

The main door faces Telok Ayer Street, under a Moorish arch with a scalloped edge made of many small curves. Mouldings of leaves and flowers decorate the wall around it. Look at the two towers again. They are cut with small niches. On some religious festivals in the past, oil lamps were set into those niches. Then walk a few steps along the Boon Tat Street side. There you will see a row of tall French style windows, each topped with a half round fanlight.

The front towers have been part of this street view for a long time. They can be clearly picked out in a painting of the area made in 1856 by the artist Percy Carpenter, looking down from a hill called Mount Wallich.

Running a shrine meant looking after money and property, and that brought the courts in. In 1893, a court appointed five trustees to manage the Nagore Dargah together with the Jamae Mosque. A new panel was chosen in 1910, and it took on Al-Abrar Mosque as well. That mosque, which began around 1827 as a thatched hut, stands a short walk along this same street. The three sites formed an endowment, known as a wakaf, and in 1917 their care passed to the Mahomedan and Hindu Endowment Board.

After 1968, ownership passed to the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore, known as Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura, or MUIS. On 19 November 1974, the shrine was gazetted as a national monument.

The building had an unexpected second life in the 1990s. In 1994, the nearby Moulana Mosque was pulled down to make room for the UOB Plaza tower, and its worshippers needed somewhere to pray. For a time, this shrine served as their mosque, and it was even registered under the name Masjid Moulana Mohamed Ali. When a new mosque for them was completed close by in 1995, daily prayers moved there. By 1996, the old shrine had fallen into poor condition and was locked up to keep the public safe.

Its future was settled in May 2005, when MUIS confirmed that the building would become a heritage centre. After major repairs, it reopened on 29 May 2011, opened by President S R Nathan. The two keramats and other religious fittings were taken out during the 2010s, and a further round of work ran from 2013 until early 2015. The old prayer hall has been kept, though it is no longer used for prayer. The centre now tells the story of Indian Muslims in Singapore and what they gave to the country.

At the opening in 2011, the minister in charge of Muslim affairs, Yaacob Ibrahim, put it simply. This, he said, was where the Indian Muslims had landed, and where they had made their place in Singapore. Stand at the corner for a moment and look along the street towards the old shoreline. The sea has gone, but the shrine that travellers built to thank a saint of safe voyages still stands on the street where they came ashore.

title: Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church: a Chinese roof on a Western church
transcript:
Look up at the top of the building on this corner. Above the arches and the plain upper walls, at the front, sits an open pavilion with a curved roof in the traditional Chinese manner. It looks as if a small piece of a Chinese garden had been lifted onto a European church. That mix is the whole point of this place. This is Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church, the first church in Singapore set up only for Chinese Methodists.

The story starts with a doctor. Methodist missionaries first arrived in Singapore in 1885, led by William Oldham and James Thoburn. Two years later, an American medical doctor named Benjamin West came out with his wife. He taught for a short time at the Anglo-Chinese School on Amoy Street, then moved into Chinatown.

In 1889, West opened a clinic in a shophouse on Upper Nankin Street. That street no longer exists. Its site is now Hong Lim Park, not far from here. Soon he was using the same shophouse for Sunday worship. About thirty people came. Hokkien was the language they heard, and the church's records say some of them were West's own patients, men recovering from opium addiction. That small room is counted as the beginning of this congregation.

The early worshippers were mostly Hokkien and Foochow speakers. As the Foochow group grew, it left to start its own church, the Foochow Methodist Church. Those who stayed behind were mainly Hokkien, and the congregation came to be known as the Telok Ayer Church. In 1905, the shophouse was falling apart, and the church moved to Japan Street, which today is called Boon Tat Street.

Then, in 1913, the pastor, Reverend F. H. Sullivan, bought the plot you are looking at now, at the junction of Telok Ayer Street and Cecil Street. For a while there was no building at all. Services were held under a tent on the empty land, until the tent gave way. While a simple hut of wood and corrugated iron went up on the site, the congregation met each week at Fairfield Girls' School on Neil Road. The church's own history says the hut measured only about six metres by ten.

A permanent church was planned from 1921, after more land next door was bought. Bishop George Bickley laid the foundation stone on 19 January 1924. A year later, on 11 January 1925, his successor, Bishop Titus Lowe, dedicated the finished sanctuary. Some accounts give 1924 as the year of the building and others 1925, because the work spanned both.

The design came from the firm of Swan and Maclaren. The National Heritage Board names the architect as Denis Santry, the same man behind the Cenotaph, the Sultan Mosque and the old Tanjong Pagar railway station. The church's history names the builders as a French firm, Bross and Mogin.

Now take a closer look. The body of the building is Western. It is a rectangular block resting on rows of arches. Walk along the covered five foot way at ground level and look at the piers and columns. Their rounded tops carry small crosses, a detail borrowed from Byzantine churches. Many of the doors and windows are fitted with louvres.

Then there is the pavilion on the roof. The church's own history explains why it is there. A Chinese style roof on a Roman style building was meant to speak to Chinese migrants, so they could see the church as their own.

The church also sits upside down compared with many others. The ground floor holds a social hall named after Benjamin West. The sanctuary, where people worship, is on the second storey. That is unusual for a church here, though it was common in European city churches at the time. The church believes it may have been the first in Singapore to use this layout.

In its early years, the church did more than hold services. It helped members who could not read or write to send letters home to their families in China. In 1935, John Sung, a well known evangelist from China, held revival meetings here. The pulpit he preached from has been kept.

Then came the war. When Japanese forces attacked Singapore, the walls along the five foot way were made thicker, to stop stray bullets and shrapnel. Around three hundred people took shelter inside. One long serving member later recalled a small storeroom with a trapdoor, where women and girls hid from the Japanese. He also spoke of a telescope on the roof, used to watch for an attack that was expected from the sea. Through the Japanese Occupation, from 1942 to 1945, Sunday services carried on.

That sea used to be very close. In the early nineteenth century, Telok Ayer Street ran along the shore of Telok Ayer Bay, and boats full of immigrants landed here. From the late eighteen hundreds, the British reclaimed land from the bay. The street ended up four streets inland. Cecil Street, right beside the church, was built on that reclaimed land, along with Robinson Road and Shenton Way beyond it.

On 23 March 1989, the government named the church a national monument. That was the same year the congregation marked its hundredth anniversary. A careful restoration followed, from October 1993 to August 1995, at a cost of about three million dollars. A member who oversaw the work later said the original plans could not be found, so every detail had to be studied on site.

The restoration brought a surprise. Behind the altar, under wooden boards, workers found four old timber panels. They carry Chinese characters in gold leaf that read Shangdi shi ai, which means God is Love. Nobody is sure why they had been covered up. Around the walls of the sanctuary are six more characters. They stand for respect, piety, holiness, faith, benevolence and tolerance, values that belong both to the Christian faith and to Chinese tradition.

As the congregation grew, it built a second church on Wishart Road, off Telok Blangah Road, finished in 2004. But this corner building is where it put down roots. Telok Ayer Street holds six national monuments, and this church sits among temples, a mosque and a clan hall built by other migrants. Before you move on, look up once more at that pavilion roof, placed there a century ago so that newcomers from China would know this church was meant for them.

title: Fuk Tak Chi Temple: the shrine by the sea
transcript:
Look down Telok Ayer Street and you will see offices, shophouses and new buildings, but no water. Yet the street takes its name from Telok Ayer Bay. It began as a coastal road beside that bay, and this small building in front of you once faced the sea. It is called Fuk Tak Chi, and it is also known as Fook Tet Soo Khek. Today it is the Fuk Tak Chi Museum, but for well over a century it was a working temple.

Start with the name. Its Chinese name is given as meaning something like Tua Pek Kong temple by the seaside. Tua Pek Kong is an earth deity, also known as Dai Bak Gong in Cantonese. He is said to be popular with Chinese of all dialect groups. Here, he was the heart of the temple.

Now, the date. Sources do not agree on every detail, so it helps to be careful. One account says Cantonese and Hakka immigrants set up a simple shrine here between 1820 and 1824. Roots gives 1824 as the year it began. What seems firm is an old plaque. It is dated to the fourth year of the Daoguang Emperor, which is 1824, and it carries the words Zepi haidao, which mean benefitting the island. It is described as the earliest known artefact of the Chinese community in Singapore. So by 1824, people were already worshipping on this shore.

There is an older story too. One account says a modest shrine to Tua Pek Kong stood by the sea even earlier. In that story, the body of an elder washed ashore on the original coastline here, and local people raised money to bury him on the spot. As the place gained a reputation, immigrant groups pooled funds to build a temple. Treat this as tradition rather than proven history.

Who built it is also told in slightly different ways. Most sources say the Cantonese and Hakka communities together. One says the Cantonese built it first and the Hakkas joined later. One heritage account credits the Hakka alone. Either way, this was a shared place. It has been described as an early example of the Hakka and Cantonese communities working together.

Imagine the setting. In those years the sea reached close to this street. Telok Ayer was the landing place for many Chinese immigrants, and Telok Ayer Street was set aside for the Chinese community in 1822. The shrine's purpose was simple. Newly arrived immigrants came to give thanks for a safe passage. Keep that in mind as you look at the front of the building.

The shrine did not stay simple. Donations paid for a brick temple, completed in 1825 according to some accounts. Surviving inscriptions record renovations or expansions in 1854, 1862 and 1869. The 1869 work was paid for by Cheang Hong Lim, a Hokkien businessman, so support came from beyond the two founding groups. An inscription from 1870 records a walled platform built in front of the temple, where performances were staged as offerings to the deities. That platform faced the sea.

Three associations stood behind the temple. Kwong Wai Siew represented people from Guangzhou, Huizhou and Zhaoqing. Fong Yun Thai represented people from Fengshun, Dabu and Yongding. And the Kar Yeng Five Districts brought together people from five districts including Meixian. The temple looked after two cemeteries, Cheng San Teng and Loke Yah Teng. It also worked as a community association, with a role in welfare and in settling disputes.

Running a shared temple was not always easy. In 1886 a quarrel broke out between the temple's two keepers over how money was divided. It grew serious enough to involve the colonial Inspector General and the Protector of the Chinese. On 2 January 1887 both sides signed a contract. From then on, the Cantonese and Hakka communities took turns appointing the temple keeper, and the keeper for the year carried responsibility for profits and losses. The same system of taking turns is still used by the association that looks after the temple's heritage today.

Meanwhile, the shoreline was disappearing. In the 1860s local businessmen asked the governor for permission to reclaim Telok Ayer Bay, and the request was refused. Reclamation went ahead between 1878 and 1885. Earth from nearby hills, including Mount Wallich, was used to fill the bay. Before that, boats had moored in the bay to collect fresh water, which was carried from a well at Ann Siang Hill by bullock cart. Afterwards, new land and new buildings stood between the temple and the water.

The twentieth century brought a different change. In 1985 the government requisitioned the temple. It officially closed in 1994. Taoist priests performed rituals to permanently remove the statues. The images of Tua Pek Kong and the City God, Cheng Huang Ye, were moved to an association in Geylang. In 1995 the Urban Redevelopment Authority awarded the temple, along with a free school and other shophouses, to the Far East Organization for conservation and reuse.

That led to the building you see now. It was restored in 1998 by craftsmen from China and Malaysia and reopened as the Fuk Tak Chi Museum. It has been described as Singapore's first street museum, with artefacts about the lives of early Chinese migrants. In 2000 it became part of the Far East Square development. Thian Hock Keng, another old temple from the days when this street faced the sea, is a short walk along Telok Ayer Street.

Take a last look at the temple front. It is a small building with larger ones around it. What remains of the temple today is its outer structure and the inscriptions on its inner walls. The statues have gone. The sea has gone. But the building still holds a record of how two communities built a shared place on the shoreline.

title: Ying Fo Fui Kun: the Hakka house on the old shoreline
transcript:
Look down the length of Telok Ayer Street and ask yourself where the sea went. Today the water is a long way off. But this street began as a coastal road along Telok Ayer Bay, and it took its name from that bay. In 1822, Stamford Raffles set this area aside mainly for the Chinese community, and it became the main landing site for Chinese immigrants.

Before the land was reclaimed, boats moored in the bay while they waited for fresh water, which was carried by bullock cart from a well at Ann Siang Hill. Between 1878 and 1885, the bay was filled in with earth taken from coastal hills, including Mount Wallich. One account says the street ended up four streets away from the seafront. Another says that the great temple down the road ended up five blocks from the sea. Even around the 1900s, the beach of the Telok Ayer Basin was busy with shipbuilding, as workers repaired vessels and put together light wooden boats called tongkangs.

The building in front of you, at number 98, is Ying Fo Fui Kun, a Hakka clan association and one of the oldest in Singapore. One account says its clan house was among the first buildings in Telok Ayer, where the island's earliest Chinese settlements were found, and that the association began life as a temple.

To understand why it exists, think about what a newcomer needed. On stepping ashore, finding somewhere to stay and someone to help you find work would have been a priority. Some also stopped at makeshift shrines along the waterfront to give thanks for a safe passage.

Studies of Singapore's clan associations make the same point. Most early Chinese migrants arrived virtually penniless, with no work, no lodging and no friends. Clan associations answered those needs. They helped people settle and find jobs. They looked after the sick, the destitute and widows. They organised shared social and religious activities, and they stepped in to settle disputes inside the community. One of their most important services was funerals. One study counted 200 Chinese clan associations in Singapore, and more than ninety percent of them were set up before 1960. It adds that the British administration left the different communities to run their own affairs, which made such associations necessary.

Ying Fo Fui Kun was one of the earliest. A group of Hakka clansmen founded it in 1822, though one account gives 1822 to 1823. That is about three years after Raffles landed. The man who led them is known as Liew Lok Teck, also written Liu Runde. One account says he hoped it would be more than a welfare body. He wanted it to be a kinship bridge between the Hakka in Singapore and China.

The word Hakka means guest families. The Hakka reached southern China later than other southern Han Chinese groups, and they often had to settle on poorer land. In early Singapore, the Hakkas were one of five main Chinese dialect groups, alongside the Hokkiens, Teochews, Cantonese and Hainanese. There were fewer of them than the other groups, yet theirs was one of the first to found a clan association. Most Hakkas worked as woodcutters and carpenters, or as blacksmiths and goldsmiths.

The first building was a single storey structure, and it served Hakka from five counties of Guangdong province. The association's name, Ying He, reflects its founders' wish for peaceful coexistence among the local Hakkas. By 1844, the committee judged that first building to be dilapidated. Funds were raised, and the present two storey house was built on the same site. Records differ on the date. Another account says the clan house was constructed in 1881 to 1882. All agree that it has always stayed at its original site.

Now look at the front. Two Doric columns frame the entrance, with an arch between them. The arch now carries the characters for Ying He Hui Guan. For decades it carried the name of the Ying Xin School, which the association ran inside the building from 1905 to 1970. Another account spells it Ying Sin and gives 1971.

Notice the windows on the front wall. They are set higher than a tall man's reach. One account says this was likely influenced by Hakka tu lou, the round earthen dwellings of China, where few windows sit high above the ground so intruders cannot climb in. Another says the windows were placed high to discourage intruders.

The plan follows the style of clan and temple buildings on the southeastern coast of Guangdong. A courtyard sits in the middle, surrounded by an entrance hall, a main hall and corridors. Light from the courtyard brightens the main hall by day. Granite columns hold up the second floor, where most traditional Chinese buildings would use timber. The roof structure, however, is timber. On the second level is a hall called Jia Yuan Ting, or the Hall of Fine Destiny, whose wooden roof members are painted with landscapes and scenes from Chinese mythology and folklore.

The building honours Guan Yu, the deified general of the Three Kingdoms period, also called Guan Ti. He stands for loyalty and courage. Accounts differ on whether his altar is in the main hall or upstairs.

The house also holds nineteenth century stone tablets and carved boards. The oldest surviving item is an inscribed board from 1846.

The association reached beyond this plot. In 1875 it built an extension called Wu Cheng Fu Di next door, to hold the ancestral tablets of the Hakka community. It was demolished in 1980 to widen the road. In 1887 the association bought land from the British government for burials, as its membership grew.

A renovation in 1997 restored the carved beams. On 18 December 1998, the clan house was gazetted as a national monument.

Before you walk on, find the Nagore Dargah a little way along the street. Then come back to those high windows, and the granite, and think of a community that arrived late, settled on poor land, and built this house to look after its own.

title: Jinrikisha Station: where the rickshaw trade was counted
transcript:
Look at the corner in front of you. Two roads meet at a sharp angle, and a building has been made to fit that angle exactly. It is a wedge of brick and plaster with a tower on top. This is the former Jinrikisha Station, at the meeting of Neil Road and Tanjong Pagar Road, and it was built to keep count of a trade that once filled Singapore's streets.

Start with the word. Jinrikisha is Japanese, and it means a man powered carriage. The rickshaw is generally believed to have been invented in Japan around 1869. The idea spread quickly. By 1872 there were about forty thousand in service in Japan, and China saw its first in 1873. In 1880 the first ones reached Singapore, shipped in by way of Shanghai. The rickshaw was a small, light cart with springs and large wheels, and the puller ran between its two shafts. The city took to it fast. Passengers included the well to do and British civil servants and government officials, while the men between the shafts were mostly poor immigrants. One photograph from 1900 shows a rickshaw jam outside the old Police Court on South Bridge Road. The demand was so great that Japan began making cheaper versions.

With so many vehicles on the road, the government wanted order. Accounts say a Jinricksha Ordinance was passed in 1888, and a Jinricksha Department was set up to register, license and manage both the rickshaws and the men who pulled them. Every rickshaw and every puller was meant to be known to the authorities.

This building was the answer to that need. The Municipal Council built it in 1903, although one account says it only began operating in 1904. The design is credited to the Municipal Engineer, Samuel Tomlinson, and the Municipal Architect, D M Craik. It was not just an office. It was the registration centre for rickshaws, and pullers often waited for passengers around the junction outside.

Now look at the building itself. The style is called Edwardian. The brickwork is the first thing to notice, set against white plaster mouldings. The brick was originally left bare, and the walls have since been painted. Find the corner, where the two roads meet. There you should see a curved pediment above, flanked by flat columns called Ionic pilasters. Higher up is a square tower, topped with an eight sided cupola.

Now look for the crest at the front. It is the crest of the Municipal Council, and it shows a lion standing on an island with a palm tree.

So who were the pullers? Most were newcomers from southern China. A steady flow of new arrivals, called singkeh, came because poverty and overpopulation at home were severe. Cantonese, Hengwah, Hockchia and Foochow men are all named among them. Another account says that many came from Fuzhou in Fujian province, and that the Hockchew people dominated the trade. Heritage records say many of these early Chinese immigrants endured harsh lives as pullers. They were usually barefoot, and many wore a conical hat with a flat brim.

Most did not own the vehicle. They rented it from an owner, and there were about one thousand owners by the end of the nineteenth century. Up to the 1920s, many pullers earned only around sixty cents a day, and part of that went on the rent. They lived in cramped cubicles in the shophouses of Chinatown. Rickshaws were accident prone, and pullers often suffered injuries. Many turned to opium to get through the exhaustion.

The loads could be heavy. Until 1904, most rickshaws were two seaters, with iron rimmed wheels, and a single puller might carry a family or a pile of goods. Around that year, lighter single seat models with rubber cushioned wheels appeared, and by 1919 they had replaced the older kind. The government moved against the two seaters in 1911. One account says opposition delayed the law by three years, and that it did little good in the end. Another account says the two seaters disappeared from the streets in the 1920s.

The trade could also turn tense. Martial law was declared in 1897 to end a four day strike by rickshaw workers. Later, a Rickshaw Association was formed in the 1920s to look after the pullers' welfare.

The numbers grew enormous. Sources give different figures. One says about fifty thousand rickshaws by 1920. Another says about fifty thousand pullers in that decade, with only some thirty thousand of them registered and the rest working as a kind of pirate taxi. Either way, tens of thousands of men were pulling people through these streets. Then came the change. Cycle rickshaws, or trishaws, were introduced in 1929, and within six years they outnumbered the pulled kind. In 1947, pulled rickshaws were phased out, and trishaws, trams and buses took over.

Think about the neighbourhood around you, too. Tanjong Pagar is a Malay name that means cape of stakes, probably after the stakes fishermen used to secure fish traps along this shore. The Tanjong Pagar Dock Company was formed in 1864, and wharves were built along the coast as shipping increased. The area was an enclave for thousands of Chinese and Indian dock workers who had migrated to Singapore from the mid nineteenth century. By the 1890s, two and three storey shophouses had been built on nearby Duxton Hill, and the district kept growing around the port.

The station did not stay a rickshaw office. At one point it was a family planning clinic. In 1987 the Urban Redevelopment Authority restored it, and it was one of the first buildings in Tanjong Pagar to be restored. Today it is a conserved building.

Before you walk on, look back along both roads from the narrow end of the corner. This is where one of the busiest working trades in colonial Singapore was written down, licensed and checked, one rickshaw at a time.

title: Tanjong Pagar Railway Station: the end of the line
transcript:
Look up at the front of the building. High on the facade, four pale figures look down over Keppel Road. They are part of what was once the Singapore railway station, also called Keppel Road railway station, and now known as the Former Tanjong Pagar Railway Station. For almost eighty years it was the place where Malayan trains ended and began.

To see why it is here, start with the harbour. A dock company was formed at Tanjong Pagar in 1864 and built wharves. The area was renamed Keppel Harbour in 1900. Plans for a railway through Singapore, mainly to serve that harbour, began in 1899. Trains first ran in Singapore around 1903, and the terminus then was at Tank Road, near the Former House of Tan Yeok Nee. The line was later pushed south towards Tanjong Pagar and the wharves, but it was abandoned after nearby residents complained about the noise.

Then came the Causeway across the Johor Strait. Goods trains began using it on 17 September 1923, and passenger trains followed on 1 October, though one account gives 1924 for the opening. Before the Causeway, passengers and goods had to change at Woodlands onto a ferry to Johor Bahru, and then take a connecting train. Once the Causeway opened, traffic between Singapore and Malaya grew sharply, and the old station at Tank Road struggled to cope.

Plans to rebuild Tank Road were dropped. Instead, the British administration chose a site near the docks. That meant goods from the Malayan interior could reach the harbour quickly. At the opening, John Strachan said the new terminus had architectural features more worthy of the city of Singapore than the shed at Tank Road.

A new route was needed to reach the site. A nine mile deviation was drawn up mainly to stop trains running along Bukit Timah Road, which was prone to flooding. Construction of the station began on 7 May 1929. By August 1931, over 630 concrete piles had been driven into the ground. The old line was later taken up, and some of that land became roads, including Clemenceau Avenue. The station work was supervised by John Strachan, who was general manager and chief engineer of the Federated Malay States Railways.

The station opened in 1932. Sir Cecil Clementi, the governor, officiated. Most accounts give the date as 2 May, though one says the station was completed on 3 May. Either way, the building became the southern terminus of the Federated Malay States Railways.

The design came from three architects at the firm Swan and Maclaren. Their names were H. C. Atkin Berry, Denis Santry and D. S. Petrovich. They drew ideas from railway stations in England. Santry also designed the Cenotaph, the Sultan Mosque and the Telok Ayer Chinese Methodist Church.

The style is mostly Art Deco. Look for geometric shapes and stylised flowers in the decoration. Both are used generously.

Now return to those four figures on the front. They are marble sculptures by Angiolo Vannetti, a sculptor from Florence in Italy. Each is an allegory of one of the main parts of the Malayan economy. The themes are agriculture, industry, commerce and transport. Above them, you can see the letters F, M, S and R. They stand for the Federated Malayan States Railways.

The roofs hold a surprise. They are covered in circular and triangular tiles, called wa dang and di shui in Chinese. Tiles like these are usually found on Chinese buildings and temples. Here they sit on a railway station designed by European architects, and they carry stylised Chinese characters for long life. Borrowing local building elements in this way was another habit of Art Deco.

Step inside, if you can, and look at the central hall. It is 22 metres high and has no supporting columns, so nothing blocks the view. Overhead is a reinforced concrete barrel vault, described as a major engineering feat of its day, and the hall was lit and ventilated naturally.

Tall murals line the walls. They are made of approximately 9,000 ceramic tiles and were crafted by William Rowe of Doulton and Company, which is now Royal Doulton. They show the work that made Malaya rich. You can see rubber tapping, tin mining, rice growing and different kinds of transport. At either end of the hall, look for the coats of arms of the Straits Settlements and of the Federated Malay States.

Even the floor was designed with passengers in mind. The wall panels and original floor slabs were made locally, using rubber to deaden noise. Outside, behind the main building, the platforms were long enough for the longest mail trains. They were covered by roofs of reinforced concrete, shaped like umbrellas.

This was never just a place to catch a train. The upper floors of the main hall held a station hotel. Over the years the building also held a hair salon, a restaurant, and a pub and lounge called the Prairie Express. In 1936, a bookshop called the Habib Railway Book Store opened inside.

The trains themselves ran a long way. In its last years, the line offered six daily intercity services to Kuala Lumpur, and other trains reached states such as Kelantan, in the northeast of Peninsular Malaysia.

The future of the station was argued over for years. In 1990, Malaysia and Singapore signed an agreement about it. Malaysia would move the station to Bukit Timah, and the railway land at Tanjong Pagar would go to a jointly owned company, with sixty percent held by Malaysia and forty percent by Singapore. But the two sides read the agreement differently. Singapore said it took effect at once. Malaysia said it applied only after Malaysia chose to move. The question was settled in a joint statement on 24 May 2010.

The final chapter came in 2011. The station stayed in operation until 30 June 2011, though one account gives 1 July as the day services ended. Sultan Ibrahim of Johor drove the last train out. His grandfather had opened the Causeway in 1923, and the Sultan learned to drive a train, with training from the railway, before he took the controls. On the same day, Malaysia returned the land to Singapore, and the terminus moved north to Woodlands.

Before that, on 9 April 2011, the main building was gazetted as a national monument.

Take a last look at the facade before you walk on. The trains no longer come here, but the four figures are still in place. Agriculture, industry, commerce and transport were what the railway carried, and they still face Keppel Road.

title: UOB Innovation Hub: the towers once called The Hive
transcript:
Look up at the cluster of rounded towers in front of you. Each one is wider at the top than at the bottom, and each is wrapped in ribbed, earthy concrete that looks almost hand moulded. The building soon picked up a nickname: the dim sum basket building, after the round steamer baskets stacked on tables in Chinese restaurants. Once you have heard it, it is hard to see anything else.

The building has gone by several names. When it opened in 2015 it was called The Hive. The university also knew it as Learning Hub South. In March 2026 it was renamed the UOB Innovation Hub.

Before looking closer, it helps to know where you are. This is the main campus of Nanyang Technological University, usually called NTU, in the west of Singapore. In 1955 a Chinese language university called Nanyang University was founded just to the south of this spot, on land donated by the Hokkien Huay Kuan, a clan association. In 1980 it merged into what became the National University of Singapore, and in 1981 a new engineering school, the Nanyang Technological Institute, took over the grounds. Ten years later, on 1 July 1991, that institute became Nanyang Technological University. If you walk south through the campus, the old Nanyang University administration building still stands, now home to the Chinese Heritage Centre and a national monument.

The layout of the campus around you was planned in the early 1980s by the Japanese architect Kenzo Tange, who later won the Pritzker Prize. His plan set buildings among large green spaces.

The new building came out of a competition, won by the London studio of the British designer Thomas Heatherwick. He is perhaps best known for the cauldron that held the Olympic flame at the London Games in 2012. This was his studio's first major building in Asia. It worked with a local firm, CPG Consultants, which led the construction. The project was part of a larger campus scheme, and it was described at the time as the first redevelopment of the campus in twenty years.

The brief was a question as much as a design problem. If students can find lectures, books and experts on the internet from their own bedrooms, why should they come to a university building at all? Heatherwick's studio answered that the campus now mattered most as a place to meet people. Its target was the old model of box shaped classrooms lined up along long, dim corridors. The studio wanted a building with no corridors at all, one that would make students and teachers run into each other as often as possible.

So look again at how the towers are arranged. There are twelve of them, each eight storeys tall, standing in a ring around a shared central atrium. There is no single front door. At ground level the building is open on all sides, so you can walk in from almost any direction and arrive in the same shared space. The atrium is naturally ventilated, so air moves through it without being sealed in.

The classrooms themselves are unusual. There are 56 of them, and they are rounded, with no corners. That was deliberate. A square room has a front, where the teacher stands, and a back. The designers wanted rooms where nobody sits at the head of the class, and where students work together around shared tables while the tutor acts more like a guide. Every room faces the atrium.

Between the classrooms are balconies, small nooks and garden spaces, roughly as much space again as the classrooms themselves, meant for stopping and talking. The balconies grow larger towards the top. Plants and trees were placed on the roof and on some of the circulation levels, a nod to Tange's green campus.

Now step closer to the walls. The studio chose reinforced concrete and then set out to treat it like clay, giving it detail and warmth that people do not expect from concrete. The curved panels have irregular horizontal stripes, cast using ten adjustable silicone moulds. One architecture magazine thought the towers looked like giant parsnips. The designers preferred to compare the texture to wet clay. The towers are lifted off the ground on 61 angled concrete columns, and their surfaces ripple too.

Look at the concrete walls around the stairs and lifts, slotted in between the towers. They carry around seven hundred drawings by the British illustrator Sara Fanelli. They show images from science, art and literature. In 2013, before it was even finished, the project received Green Mark Platinum, the top rating in Singapore's green building scheme.

The building took 32 months to build and cost 45 million Singapore dollars. It was unveiled in March 2015, ahead of the new academic year that August. Its official opening came on 20 October 2015, when it was opened by Ong Ye Kung, then Acting Minister for Education. The building was tied to a change in teaching that NTU called the flipped classroom. Students watched lectures online before class, and time in the room was used for discussion, debate and team work. The university planned to move about 1,500 courses to this approach within five years. A second learning hub was already being built.

Not everyone was won over. Reviews were mixed. One British architecture magazine admired much of the building but found that parts of it felt like a lonely car park. Even so, The Hive went on to draw a steady stream of visitors with cameras, and it was shortlisted at the World Architecture Festival in 2015.

The latest chapter began on 25 March 2026. The building took the name of the bank UOB, and its lower floors were turned into subsidised offices for start ups linked to the university, backed by money from UOB and the Wee Foundation. The change was not quiet. Many students, especially from the humanities and social sciences, the building's main users, objected to losing rooms and to losing the old name.

Before you leave, stand in the middle of the atrium and turn slowly in a full circle. Twelve towers, no front, no back, no corridor. Whatever the sign outside says, the building was designed around one idea: that a university is most useful when people keep bumping into each other.

title: Chinese Heritage Centre: the old heart of Nantah
transcript:
Find the building with the great curved Chinese roof, sitting above a broad body of reinforced concrete, with a garden spread out in front of it. That garden is Yunnan Garden, and the building is the former library and administration block of Nanyang University. Today it is home to the Chinese Heritage Centre, a research institute of Nanyang Technological University devoted to the study of Chinese communities living outside China. To understand why that institute sits here, in this particular building, you need the story of the university that came first.

Nanyang University was known to almost everyone by its short name, Nantah. It was the first Chinese language university in Southeast Asia, and only the second university of any kind in Singapore. In 1953 the rubber magnate Tan Lark Sye, a leader of the Hokkien community, proposed a university of their own. He gave five million dollars himself. The Hokkien Huay Kuan, the clan association he led, gave more than five hundred acres of land out here in Jurong, which was then mostly rural.

What made the appeal remarkable was who answered it. Money came from wealthy merchants, but also from trishaw riders, hawkers, cabaret girls and washerwomen. The university was meant to train teachers for Chinese schools across Malaya, and to keep Chinese culture and learning alive in the region. For many ordinary families, giving to Nantah was a way of opening a door for the next generation.

Building work on the campus began in the middle of the 1950s. While it went on, the first students took preparatory classes at two Chinese secondary schools. In March 1956, the university flag was raised in a simple ceremony on the new campus to mark the start of lessons. The official opening came two years later, on 30 March 1958, and around fifty thousand well wishers are said to have turned up for it.

Now look closely at the building itself. Its architect was Ng Keng Siang, a local architect who also designed the Lim Bo Seng Memorial on the Esplanade. The style is called the Chinese National style, and a BiblioAsia article places it in a wider movement known as Chinese Renaissance architecture. The idea was to join a modern frame of reinforced concrete with a roof that is unmistakably Chinese. In the years around the end of colonial rule, buildings like this were a way of saying that a modern institution could also look like it belonged to its own community.

The details reward a slow look. Along the edges of the roof are rows of round eaves tiles and triangular drip tiles. They carry two Chinese characters, nan and da, the short form of the university's name. On either side of the central block, the side wings show their brick faces openly. When it was new, this was the university library. In 1966 it took on a new role as the administration block, and that is the name it kept.

Out in the garden, look for two more pieces of the old university. One is the memorial, a tower with a double tier Chinese roof, standing on an eight sided base with steps on all four sides. It marks the completion of the first phase of building, and the colonial governor, Sir William Goode, unveiled it in 1958. The other is a gateway arch bearing the university's name. The one here is a copy. The original arch, the old entrance to the campus, still stands some distance away in the housing estates of Jurong West, cut off from the campus by the Pan Island Expressway.

Nantah's life was never easy. In 1959 an official commission criticised its staffing, facilities and curriculum, and declined to recommend that the government recognise its degrees. Further reviews followed. In 1965 a committee chaired by the historian Wang Gungwu looked at the curriculum, and its recommendations led to protests and class boycotts by students. The university also widened its reach. A Department of Malay Studies opened in 1968 and drew Malay students to the campus.

By the 1970s, many students were attending English language schools, and enrolment at Nantah suffered. In 1979 the government invited the British academic Sir Frederick Dainton to advise on university education. He proposed bringing Nanyang University and the University of Singapore together. The merger went ahead in 1980, creating the National University of Singapore. Nantah held its last graduation ceremony that August.

For a short time the campus stood empty. Then, in the early 1980s, a new body called Nanyang Technological Institute moved in. Around the start of the 1990s it became a full university and took the name it has today, Nanyang Technological University. So the campus you are standing on carries two names in its history: Nanyang University, the Chinese language university the community built, and Nanyang Technological University, the English language university that grew up in its place.

The building in front of you was given a new purpose in 1995. On 17 May that year, the Chinese Heritage Centre was set up as a non profit body with an international board of business leaders, scholars and public servants. On the very same day, the replica arch in the garden was unveiled by the minister George Yeo. At the end of the 1990s, the library and administration building, the memorial and the original arch were protected together as a national monument, the highest level of protection a site can have in Singapore. Records differ slightly on the exact year.

In 2011 the centre was restructured as an autonomous institute within the university. It is described as the first and only university institute anywhere dedicated to the study of the overseas Chinese. It works as a research centre, a library and a museum, and its library carries the name of Wang Gungwu, the same historian who once reviewed Nantah's teaching. Its work documents the lives and identity of Chinese people around the world, and the history of Nantah itself.

There is a neat fit between the building and that work. Nantah itself was an overseas Chinese project, paid for by a Chinese community that wanted its own place of higher learning, far from China. The centre now studies communities like the one that raised this roof. Before you move on, look up once more at the eaves, and find those two small characters, nan and da, repeated tile after tile along the edge.

title: Nanyang University Memorial: a tower for the people who paid
transcript:
Find the small tower at the heart of the garden. It sits on an eight sided base, and short flights of steps climb up to it from four sides, one for each point of the compass. On top is a Chinese roof in two tiers, one set above the other. This is the Nanyang University Memorial, also known as the Former Nanyang University Memorial. It is modest in size, but it carries one of the great fundraising stories in Singapore's history.

Take a moment to look around before we begin. You are in Yunnan Garden, on the campus of Nanyang Technological University in Jurong West. On the higher ground nearby stands the old library and administration building of Nanyang University, with its own sweeping Chinese roof. The memorial was placed in the garden in front of it, and the two belong to the same story.

That story starts in 1953, with a Hokkien rubber magnate named Tan Lark Sye. He chaired the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and was president of the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan. Early in 1953 he proposed a university for the Chinese community, one that would teach in Chinese.

The plan had several goals. It would give Chinese educated young people a proper path to higher learning. It would protect and pass on Chinese culture and values. And it would train teachers for the high schools of Malaya. The new school would be called Nanyang University, and people soon gave it an affectionate short name, Nantah.

Money and land came next. Tan Lark Sye gave five million dollars of his own money. The Hokkien Huay Kuan gave a huge stretch of land in Jurong, more than five hundred acres, for the campus where you now stand. The association also helped to raise funds.

What makes this place special is who else gave. Donations came from every level of Chinese society. Wealthy merchants gave, but so did hawkers, taxi drivers and washerwomen. Cabaret girls and dance hostesses gave. Trishaw riders are among the donors most often remembered. One woodblock print from the period shows trishaw riders banding together to hand over a whole day's earnings to the university fund.

This memorial was built to honour those donors. Most of them were ordinary working people. The tower is a thank you to all of them at once.

Building work on the campus began in 1954. The architect for the first phase was Ng Keng Siang, one of the first Singapore born architects with a university training. He had studied in London and New York, and he ran one of the most successful practices in the colony. His other work includes the Asia Insurance Building in the city and the Lim Bo Seng Memorial in Esplanade Park.

For Nantah, Ng used a style known as the Chinese National style. Look closely at the memorial and you can see how it works. The body of the structure is modern reinforced concrete. On top sits a roof in a distinctly Chinese form. The idea was to marry the new building methods of the day with a look that spoke of Chinese tradition. The library building and the university's entrance arch were designed in the same style, so the three structures look like members of one family.

While the campus was being built, students did not wait. Preparatory classes were held at two Chinese schools in town, The Chinese High School and Chung Cheng High School. Then, on 15 March 1956, the university flag was raised on the new campus in a simple ceremony, marking the start of classes. The first intake was 584 students, spread across three faculties: arts, science and commerce.

The grand day came two years later. On 30 March 1958, Nanyang University held its official opening. A crowd of around fifty thousand well wishers came out to Jurong to see it. On the same day this memorial was unveiled, marking the end of the first phase of building. The Governor of Singapore, Sir William Goode, performed the unveiling at a ceremony with more than a hundred guests. Some accounts say Tan Lark Sye stood beside him.

The first class of graduates, 437 of them, left the university in 1959. By 1963, enrolment had grown to 2,324 students. In 1980, it was merged by law with the University of Singapore to form the National University of Singapore. The Nantah campus fell quiet. Records differ slightly on dates, but within a year or two a new institution, the Nanyang Technological Institute, moved onto the grounds. It later grew into the university that occupies this campus today, Nanyang Technological University. In 1996, the alumni rolls of the old Nanyang University were transferred to NTU, tying the two institutions together on paper as well as on the ground.

In 1998, the memorial was gazetted as a national monument, together with the old library and administration building and the original entrance arch. The three structures were protected as a single monument. That is the highest level of protection a building can receive in Singapore.

The garden around the memorial has also changed. It was recently reworked as part of a project to renew Yunnan Garden, which linked the plaza in front of the old library, the garden itself and Nanyang Lake into one connected landscape. The memorial was restored during that work.

Before you move on, walk once around the base. Notice how the steps rise from four directions, so the tower can be approached from any side. Look up at the two layers of roof, and at how small the whole structure is beside the trees and lawns. Then think about the crowd that stood out here in 1958, and the trishaw riders who handed over a whole day's earnings so that a campus could rise on this land. This tower was put up to remember them.

title: Nantah Arch: a gateway remembered twice
transcript:
Find the gateway with the sweeping Chinese roof at the edge of Yunnan Garden. Start with the most useful fact. The arch in front of you is a copy. The original still stands, but not on this campus. It is on the other side of the Pan-Island Expressway, at Jurong West Street 93, among the housing blocks. This one was built because the original ended up cut off from the campus. It was unveiled on 17 May 1995 by George Yeo, who was then Minister for Information and the Arts.

So why build a second arch at all? To answer that, you need the story of the university it once welcomed people into. Its name was Nanyang University, and most people knew it by a shorter name, Nantah.

In 1953, a Hokkien rubber magnate and philanthropist named Tan Lark Sye proposed that the Chinese community should have a university of its own, one that taught in Chinese. He was then leading the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan, the Hokkien clan association, and he backed the idea with a personal gift of five million dollars. The clan association gave a large piece of land in Jurong, much of it a rubber plantation, as the site. Records differ on its exact size, but it was hundreds of acres in the west of the island, then mostly undeveloped.

Then came the fundraising. The money did not only come from the rich. Trishaw riders, cabaret girls and washerwomen gave what they could. Taxi drivers and trishaw pullers gave charity rides. Dance hostesses held charity dances, and hawkers sold charity meals. The campaign reached well beyond Singapore, to the Malay Peninsula, Sarawak, North Borneo and Indonesia. The university was, in a real sense, paid for by a whole community.

Building began in 1954. The local architect Ng Keng Siang was appointed for the first phase, and the arch was completed around 1955. It was designed in what is called the Chinese National style. That style mixes old and new. A distinctly Chinese roof sits on top of a modern frame of reinforced concrete. Look up at the roof in front of you and you can see the idea. The shape is old. The structure underneath it is not.

On the original arch, the name of the university is set boldly across the central beam, together with the year the university opened. One account says the four large characters of the name were written by the noted calligrapher Yu Youren. The arch was the front door of the campus. Cars and buses once drove through it from Old Upper Jurong Road on their way into the university.

Before the campus was ready, the first preparatory lessons were held at two Chinese schools, The Chinese High School and Chung Cheng High School. Then, on 15 March 1956, the university flag was raised at the new campus in a simple ceremony, and teaching began that month with a first group of 584 students. The grand official opening followed on 30 March 1958. On that day, cars and crowds are said to have filled the roads all the way from here in Jurong to Newton Circus in town.

Nantah's life was not easy. For years its degrees were not formally recognised by the government, which only agreed to recognise them in 1968. As more students attended English language schools, the university came under pressure to change. In time, apart from Chinese language and Chinese history, its classes were taught in English.

The end came in 1980. On 5 April that year, Nanyang University merged with the University of Singapore, and on 8 August the combined body was launched as the National University of Singapore. The teaching moved away, and the campus here stood empty for a time. Over its life, Nantah had educated around 12,000 students from Singapore, Malaysia and further afield.

In the early 1980s, a new body called Nanyang Technological Institute moved onto the old grounds. Records differ on whether it started in 1981 or 1982. In 1991 the institute became Nanyang Technological University, the NTU around you now. It took over the old grounds and carries a similar name.

Now turn and look behind the arch. The building with the large Chinese roof is the former Nanyang University Library and Administration Building. The replica was placed here, in front of it, on purpose. If you look closely at the ends of the roof tiles on that building, you may spot the round eaves tiles and the pointed drip tiles. They are stamped with two Chinese characters, nan and da, the short form of the university's name. The same marks were used on the tiles of the original arch.

In 1998, the original arch, the library building and a memorial in this garden were gazetted together as a single national monument. Notice the wording. The protected arch is the one out in Jurong West, not the copy you are looking at. This replica stands in for it, and keeps its outline in the place where the old campus once had its heart.

The original has had its own recent chapter. Its green glazed roof tiles had faded and been damaged by around seventy years of sun and rain. A major restoration began in 2024. After consulting the National Heritage Board, the restorers replaced the old tiles with identical new ones. Some of the original tiles went into the care of the NTU Museum, so a few pieces of the first arch have come back to campus after all.

If you have time later, the original is worth the short trip. It stands in the same spot it always has. What changed was everything around it. The old campus land around it is now a residential area, and an expressway now runs between the gateway and the garden it used to open onto.

Before you walk on, take one more look at the arch in front of you. It is not old, and it was never the campus entrance. But it was built for a reason. When the original was cut off from the campus, people wanted a gateway they could still stand under here, beside the library, the memorial and the garden. That is what this copy gives them: a way to keep Nantah's front door in view.

title: Yunnan Garden: the green heart of old Nantah
transcript:
Find the stairs on the western side of the garden, near the humanities building, and walk down. At the bottom you meet a small Chinese pavilion with a green tiled roof and red beams. Past it, the ground opens up into lawns, bamboo, little streams and winding paths. This is Yunnan Garden. It was once the heart of a university that no longer exists, and today it sits within the campus of Nanyang Technological University.

The numbers give you a sense of scale. The garden and its surrounds now form a heritage precinct of about nine hectares. That is bigger than twelve football fields. Keep that in mind as you explore, because the paths will carry you a long way from where you started.

The name has spread far beyond these lawns. In Chinese, people often call this whole campus Yunnan Garden, or simply Nantah, the short form of Nanyang University. Outside the campus gates, Yunnan is also the name of a subzone of Jurong West, and there is a Yunnan Park out on Jurong West Street 93.

To understand why a garden like this sits out here, picture Jurong before the university came. Like much of rural Singapore, it was covered in plantations, mainly gambier and rubber. Jurong Road was once the only road leading to the south west of the island, and it had just two lanes. Villagers used its milestones to describe where they lived.

In 1953, a Hokkien rubber magnate named Tan Lark Sye proposed something new for the Chinese community: a university of its own. He led the Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan, the clan association of the Hokkien people, and also chaired the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. He and other community leaders wanted a place of higher learning for Chinese educated students, and a way to keep Chinese culture alive in Malaya. The university was also meant to train high school teachers.

Tan gave five million dollars of his own money. He is said to have been inspired by the giving of another businessman, Tan Kah Kee. The Hokkien Huay Kuan gave the land, a huge parcel in western Jurong of around 500 acres, then largely undeveloped countryside. And then ordinary people joined in. Heritage accounts of the fundraising name trishaw riders, hawkers, cabaret girls, washerwomen and dance hostesses, alongside millionaires, all giving what they could.

Building began in 1954. The architect for the first phase was a local man, Ng Keng Siang. He worked in what is called the Chinese National style, which puts a distinctly Chinese roof on top of a modern concrete frame. You can see that idea repeated around this garden, in the curved roofs and the red and green colouring of the pavilions.

Lessons began around 1956. On 15 March that year, the university's flag was raised in a simple ceremony on the new campus. One memory from those early days is that on the day the university opened, Jurong Road was so jammed that nothing could pass, and the traffic jam was said to be the biggest Singapore had seen. The official opening came on 30 March 1958, when about fifty thousand well wishers gathered here.

At the centre of this garden stands the Nanyang University Memorial, a tower with a double tier Chinese roof, unveiled that same day to mark the end of the first phase of building and to honour the donors.

For more than two decades, this was Nanyang University. It was the first Chinese language university in Southeast Asia. It added a Department of Malay Studies in 1968, which brought in Malay students, and it gave jobs to many people who lived in Jurong. And this garden sat at the centre of its grounds.

But in 1980 Nanyang University merged with the University of Singapore to form the National University of Singapore. The last convocation here took place on 16 August 1980. For a short time the grounds stood quiet. Then a new technical institute, the Nanyang Technological Institute, moved in. In the early 1990s it became a full university, Nanyang Technological University, which is the campus around you today. In 1998, three structures from the old university were gazetted together as a single national monument. And in 2019, the road in front of the old library was renamed Tan Lark Sye Walk, after the man who started it all.

Decades later, NTU set out to renew the garden. The rejuvenated Yunnan Garden opened on 13 February 2020, though some of the finishing work ran on into the next year. More than a thousand new trees from over eighty species were planted. A boardwalk, small themed gardens and a new system to manage stormwater were added. Nanyang Lake, to the north, was expanded and joined to the garden by a waterfall.

Now, walk east along the paths. Look down as you go. The tiles are laid in octagons, hexagons and triangles. Somewhere near the middle, you may find a small culinary garden, planted with edible plants such as thyme, rosemary and peppers. The pavilions along the way are good places to stop in the shade.

As you head north, you reach the waterfall, about five point six metres tall, at the northernmost point of the garden. Water from Nanyang Lake pours over it into a lower pool, and from there it feeds the little streams you passed on the way in.

Stairs on the northern side climb to the level of the top of the falls. From there, paths lead around Nanyang Lake, with views over the water.

The story of this place is still being written. In March 2026, a book edited by Associate Professor Hee Wai Siam was launched under the title Yunnan Garden, then and now. It gathers more than thirty essays in Chinese by teachers, students and alumni, set beside old black and white photographs and new colour ones. A great grandson of Tan Lark Sye came to the launch.

Before you leave, climb those northern stairs and turn around. From up there you can take in the whole sweep of the garden in one view: the pavilions, the lawns, the streams, and the land that a clan association and thousands of donors gave so that Chinese speaking students in Jurong could have a university of their own.
